en/1-getting-started/01-what-quartzhub-i.title: 1.1 – What QuartzHub is
en/1-getting-started/01-what-quartzhub-i.content:
QuartzHub is a Mac app for Quartz. Without it, you run Quartz
from the command line and edit its configuration file in a text editor; with it, you click.
What it takes off your hands
A Quartz project consists of a configuration file, a folder full of notes, a few stylesheets and a
list of installed plugins. All of it is text, and all of it
could be edited by hand. QuartzHub gives each of these a page:

Create a new project without running git and npm yourself.
Edit the configuration without writing YAML, with an explanation next to every field.
Link the content folder, also straight to an
Obsidian vault, and switch between Copy and Link
without losing a note.
Install and set up plugins from a searchable
marketplace, with a form instead of YAML.
Change colours, fonts and spacing, in layers that sit side by side in the order in which they
override each other.
Build the page grid in an editor with the mouse instead of in CSS.
Start the preview and build the site, with Quartz’s output in the same window.
Make books: a selection of pages as PDF or ePub.
Publish in several ways, with a preview of what will be transferred.
Get back when something went wrong: before larger changes QuartzHub takes a
snapshot by itself.

What it does not do
It is not an editor. Notes are written elsewhere, in Obsidian, in a text editor, anywhere.
QuartzHub does not touch what is in the content folder; it builds a website from it.
It does not replace Quartz. What appears on the finished site is up to Quartz and its plugins.
Where this handbook stops at “that is how Quartz does it”, the
Quartz documentation carries on.
It does not hide the files. Every change lands in exactly the file it would have landed in had
you made it by hand. A project set up with QuartzHub can be carried on by hand at any time, and the
other way round.
The tools behind it
Working with QuartzHub involves four programs. Only one of them needs operating.






























ProgramRoleDo you operate it?Obsidian or another editorWhere notes are written, as Markdown files in a folder.Yes, to write. Obsidian is not required, but Quartz understands its [[en/8-reference/05-glossary#WikilinkQuartzTurns the notes into a website. This is called a [[en/8-reference/05-glossary#Buildbuild]].Node and npmThe runtime Quartz works in, and its package manager.No, QuartzHub brings both.gitKeeps the history of files.Only under Git Sync and when publishing to a [[en/8-reference/05-glossary#Branch
This is how they fit together:
Obsidian ─writes─▶ vault ◀─link─ project ─Quartz builds─▶ website ─▶ server
                                    ▲                        ▲
                                    └─────── QuartzHub ──────┘

The vault need not live elsewhere. Without one, let QuartzHub create an empty content folder in the
project and write there.
Who it is for
For anyone who writes notes and wants a website made of them. No prior knowledge of Quartz is
needed, nor of git. Those who already use Quartz will find the same files, but with a preview next
to every switch and a way back when an update breaks something.

en/1-getting-started/02-installing-and-f.title: 1.2 – Installing and first run
en/1-getting-started/02-installing-and-f.content:
System requirements

macOS 26 or later.
A Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later). There is no version for Macs with an Intel processor.
Internet when creating a project (Quartz comes from GitHub), when installing plugins and when
publishing. Editing, preview and build work without.

You do not need to install Quartz, Node or npm: QuartzHub brings Node and npm, and Quartz lives
in each project. QuartzHub takes git from the system when one answers there, so your own
.gitconfig and credential helpers keep working; otherwise it uses the one it brings.
Download and install
QuartzHub comes as a DMG on the releases page.
Open the DMG and drag QuartzHub into the Applications folder.
macOS will not start QuartzHub the first time
QuartzHub is only ad hoc signed and not notarised by Apple; that would take a Developer ID
certificate. Gatekeeper, macOS’s launch check, therefore refuses the first start, saying Apple
cannot check the app. Start it once and close the message, then go to System Settings ▸ Privacy
& Security, click Open Anyway in the Security section and confirm with your login
password. Since macOS 15 the context menu (right click ▸ Open) no longer works for this.
If you like the Terminal, remove the quarantine flag macOS puts on downloaded files instead:
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/QuartzHub.app


Updating means downloading the new DMG and replacing the app in Applications. Projects, settings
and connections live outside the app and stay as they are (see
8.2).
The first run
At the first run the Projects window opens.

The Projects window at the first run: on the left the project list, still empty, with the first
steps; on the right the inspector.
The inspector on the right says what QuartzHub knows about the Mac:

Tools ready means: node, npm and git answered when asked for their version. Next to each
it says where it comes from, “in QuartzHub” or “from the system”.
If one does not answer, a note above the project list says what does not work without it: builds,
new projects, plugins from a git source, snapshots. As Node and npm are part of QuartzHub, a note
about them always means this installation is incomplete. Reinstalling QuartzHub is the quickest
fix.

Below, the inspector briefly explains what Quartz is and links to the Quartz documentation and the
plugin catalogue.
Questions from macOS
Two things macOS asks not at the first run, but when the time comes:

Local network. The first time you publish to a server on your own network (SFTP, rsync, FTP),
macOS asks whether QuartzHub may access the local network. Without that permission the
connection fails; QuartzHub then says where to grant it later: System Settings ▸ Privacy &
Security ▸ Local Network.
Keychain. QuartzHub keeps passwords and tokens for
publishing in the macOS keychain, never in a file. When a new version of QuartzHub reads an item
for the first time, macOS asks once; “Always Allow” is enough.

“Cannot check” is not “all good”
This holds in many places in QuartzHub, for the first time here: if something cannot be
determined, QuartzHub says so instead of giving the all-clear. A catalogue that could not be loaded
is not empty, and a version that could not be determined is not the latest.

en/1-getting-started/03-reading-the-wind.title: 1.3 – Reading the window
en/1-getting-started/03-reading-the-wind.content:
Every page of a project is built the same way. Having read this page, you need not learn the
controls again in parts 3 to 7.

The project window: the sidebar on the left, the page in the middle, the inspector on the right.
Two kinds of window
The Projects window lists all projects; that is where you create, open, duplicate and remove
them (2.1). Every project opens in a window of its own.
Two projects can be open side by side, and opening a project that is already open brings its window
to the front. Back to the list via Window ▸ Projects (⇧⌘0).
The sidebar
At the top: the project’s image, name and folder. Below, the pages, in the order in which you
usually set up a project:



































GroupPagesPart–Overview[[en/3-overview/indexSetupConfiguration, Plugins[[en/4-setup/indexDesignLayout, Styles, Templates[[en/5-design/indexPublishingPreview & Build, Git Sync, Documents, Publish[[en/6-publishing/indexMaintenanceUpdates, Snapshots[[en/7-maintenance/index
The button at the top left hides and shows the sidebar.
Title and history
The window’s title names the place, not the project: the page on top, below it the tab if the
page has tabs. The Window menu shows “project – page” instead, so two project windows can be
told apart.
Back and Forward at the left of the toolbar go through the window’s history, page by page
and tab by tab, as in a browser. The shortcuts are ⌘[ and ⌘]. A link to another page, such as
“Plugins ›” on the overview, is a step like any other; Back returns to where you came from. The same
commands and all pages are in the Go menu.
Tabs
Configuration, Plugins, Layout and Styles have several tabs. They sit as segments in a row of their
own above the page. When the window is too narrow for all segments, they turn into a menu named
after the chosen tab.
The inspector
On the right is the inspector, in the same place on every page. When something on the page is
selected, a row in a list, an area in a grid, it shows its details, settings and actions. When
nothing is selected, it explains the page, shows what applies to it and leads to the matching chapter
with Read this in the handbook; with a selection, Help ▸ This Page in the Handbook does. Where
the inspector saves
at once instead of waiting for Save, it says so itself.
The button at the far right of the toolbar shows and hides it, as do View ▸ Show Inspector and
⌃⌘I. That applies to the whole window, not to one page.
The toolbar
On the right of the toolbar, always in the same order:

the page’s actions as symbols, such as ➕ to create something. At most one action per page is
highlighted in colour, the one the page is mostly about, such as Start on Preview & Build;
Save, on pages that edit a file;
the button for the inspector.

Whatever applies to the whole project is also in the Project menu: Start Server (⌘R),
Stop Server (⌘.), Run build (⌘B) and Show Project Folder in Finder.
Saving
Pages that edit a file, such as Configuration and Styles, write only on Save (⌘S). The button is
only enabled when there is something to save. Unsaved changes also show as the dot in the red
button at the top left of the window.
Leaving a page with unsaved changes, through the sidebar, the history, a link, closing the window
or quitting, asks: Save, Discard changes or Cancel. If saving fails, you stay on the
page. Nothing gets lost silently.
Notes and explanations
Three kinds of text appear next to the controls:

A box with a symbol says something about the state of a thing: in the accent colour a piece of
information, orange a warning, red an error. Its text can be selected and copied, such as a path
in an error message.
A red line right below a field says what is wrong with what was just typed.
Grey text explains what a field does.

Folding and dragging
Fold groups open and close with a click anywhere in their header row, not only on the arrow.
Where a page is split into areas one above the other, such as a list with the site’s preview
below, a grip sits between them. Dragging changes the split, a double click resets it, and the
window remembers it.

en/1-getting-started/04-your-first-site.title: 1.4 – Your first site
en/1-getting-started/04-your-first-site.content:
This page walks once through everything a first site needs. Each step has a chapter of its own
later; here it is only about getting through once.
1. Create a project
In the Projects window click Create new project, or choose File ▸ New Project… (⌘N) from
any window.

The “New Quartz project” dialog.

Where should the project live? The folder in which the project folder is created, such as
“Documents”.
Name of the project folder, such as my-notes. This is only the folder’s name; the site’s
title is set later.
Base URL: the address the site is to be reachable at one day, without https://. If you do
not know it yet, leave localhost.
Where do the notes come from? For a first try, Start with an empty content folder. With an
Obsidian vault, choose Point at existing notes: the notes stay where they are and QuartzHub
reads them there (4.2).
Install the basic template gives the site a finished design: colours for light and dark,
custom page grids, fonts. With example pages adds a few pages that show what it looks like
before your own notes are there.

Create project loads Quartz from GitHub into the new folder and installs what it needs. That
takes one or two minutes. Then the new project’s window opens.
2. Read the overview
The project window opens on the Overview. Its cards say how the project is doing: whether the
dev server is running, what the site is called, whether plugins are active, when it was last built.
“All good” at the top means there is nothing to do (3.1).
3. Start the preview
Click Preview & Build in the sidebar, then Start in the toolbar (⌘R). Quartz builds the site
and keeps it ready as a preview; after a few seconds it appears in the middle of the window.

The preview in the window. At the top the width (desktop, tablet, mobile), at the bottom Quartz’s
output.
The preview rebuilds on every change, to the notes as well as to the settings. So you can write in
Obsidian and watch (6.1).
4. Title and look

Configuration ▸ Site holds the site title and the base URL; Save (⌘S) writes
them (4.1).
Styles ▸ Basics sets colours and fonts (5.5), Layout
what goes where on the page (5.2).

5. Publish
Once the preview looks right, the site goes online. Publish knows several ways: GitHub Pages, a
web space over SFTP or FTP, a folder, a webhook. Which one fits is described in
6.7.
Before changes to configuration, plugins, frames and styles and before every update, QuartzHub takes
a snapshot by itself, for the configuration at most one every 15 minutes. If something goes wrong
while setting up, it leads back to the state before (7.2).

en/1-getting-started/index.title: 1 – Getting started
en/1-getting-started/index.content:
This part assumes nothing. Anyone who writes notes and wants a website made of them is in the right
place, even without ever having heard of Quartz, git or a static site generator.

What QuartzHub is: what it takes off your hands
and what it deliberately leaves alone.
Installing and first run: what the Mac
needs and what happens the first time QuartzHub opens.
Reading the window: sidebar, inspector, history,
saving. It works the same on every page; once you know this page, you know them all.
Your first site: from an empty project to the
preview.

en/2-projects/01-the-projects-window.title: 2.1 – The Projects window
en/2-projects/01-the-projects-window.content:
The Projects window opens at start. From any other window, Window ▸ Projects (⇧⌘0) leads
back to it.

Three projects, the top one selected. On the right the inspector with its details and actions.
The rows
Each row is a project:

Image and name. The name is the name of the project folder. The image is the project image
(4.3); without one, the first letter stands on a colour.
Title and address of the site, as the configuration has them.
The folder on disk. A path too long for the row is shortened in the middle; the whole one is in
the tooltip and in the inspector.
When the project was last opened.
“Dev server on port …” while this project’s preview is running.

What was opened last comes first; projects without that date follow by name. From six projects on, a
search field appears in the toolbar; it searches name, folder and title.
QuartzHub reads the list again whenever it comes back to the front. Rename a project folder in the
Finder, and the list shows it when you switch back.
Opening
Double-clicking a row opens the project in a window of its own, as do Open in the inspector and
the Return key. If the project is open already, its window comes to the front.
The inspector
With a row selected, the inspector shows title, address and the whole folder path, and below them
the actions:

Open
Show in Finder
Duplicate… (2.4)
Remove from list…

The same commands are in a row’s context menu.
Without a selection, the inspector says whether the tools are ready
(1.2), briefly explains what Quartz is, links to
this handbook and shows what you can do in a project.
When GitHub has a newer version of QuartzHub, a band above the list names it, and Download opens
its page. Nothing is installed by itself.
New and existing
The two buttons in the toolbar create a project (➕,
2.2) or add a folder in which Quartz is already set up
(2.3). From any window, File ▸ New Project… (⌘N)
and File ▸ Open Existing Project… (⌘O) do the same.
When a folder is missing

A project whose folder is gone.
A line in orange says that something is wrong with the folder:

Folder not found. The folder was moved, renamed, or is on a volume that is not mounted right
now. For a volume, connecting it is enough. Otherwise Locate folder… in the inspector shows
QuartzHub the new place. The entry stays the same and is named after the new folder afterwards.
Not a Quartz project. The folder has no quartz.config.yaml. Such an entry cannot be opened;
it comes about when the wrong folder is chosen under “Open existing project”.

Removing from the list
Remove from list… asks once and then takes the project off the list. The folder on disk is
left untouched; opening it again brings the project back.
Two things are lost on the way, and the question names them when they apply:

A running dev server of this project is stopped.
The recipient addresses and captcha secrets of the form relay (4.9)
are deleted, because they belong to the list entry and do not live in the project folder. Adding
the project again means entering them again.

When tools are missing
If node, npm or git do not answer, a note in orange appears above the list: which tool is
missing or will not run, and what does not work without it. Node and npm are part of QuartzHub; if
they are missing, this installation is incomplete, and reinstalling QuartzHub is the quickest fix.
Check again asks the tools once more, say after installing git.

en/2-projects/02-creating-a-new-project.title: 2.2 – Creating a new project
en/2-projects/02-creating-a-new-project.content:
Create new project in the Projects window, ➕ in its toolbar or File ▸ New Project… (⌘N)
open the “New Quartz project” dialog. 1.4 goes through it
briefly for a first try; this page has every question.

The dialog with its defaults.
Place and name

Where should the project live? The folder in which the project folder is created. It starts
at the default project directory from the settings (2.5).
Name of the project folder. The folder name only; it is also the name in the project list. It
must not contain “/” and cannot be “.” or “..”. The site’s title is set later under
Configuration ▸ Site.

Below, the dialog shows which folder will be created. That folder must not exist yet; QuartzHub
creates it.
Quartz starter
Quartz brings a few starters: example pages and starting settings for a particular purpose.
default is the standard. The others (obsidian, ttrpg, blog, docs) set Quartz up
for such a purpose; what exactly they do is in the
Quartz documentation. The starter is something else than the basic
template further down.
Where do the notes come from?

Start with an empty content folder. The project folder gets a content folder of its own,
empty.
Copy existing notes. The notes from the source folder are copied into the project’s
content folder once. After that they are two separate collections: what changes in the source
folder does not arrive any more.
Point at existing notes (symbolic link). The content folder becomes a link to the source
folder, an Obsidian vault for instance. The notes stay where they are, and every change there shows
in the preview at once. QuartzHub writes nothing into the vault.

Switching between folder and link later is possible without losing a note
(4.2).
How are your [[wikilinks]] written?
Quartz has to know how a link like [[Page]] is meant:

Shortest form (like Obsidian): just the name, as long as it is unique. This is Obsidian’s
default.
Absolute (from the root folder): the path from the content folder, such as [[Folder/Page]].
Relative (from the current note).

The setting has to match the notes, or the links will not find their target. In Obsidian, this is
the setting for the format of new links.
Base URL
The address the site is to be reachable at one day, without https://, such as
notes.example.org or name.github.io/project. Quartz builds links, the RSS feed and preview images
from it. If you do not know it yet, leave localhost and fill it in later under
Configuration ▸ Site.
Basic template
Install the basic template gives the site a finished design: colours for light and dark, custom
page grids (frames), typefaces the site serves itself, and every
component styled individually. It adds the quartz-forms plugin with a contact form that sends
nothing yet (4.9).
With example pages adds a few pages that show what the site looks like before your own notes are
there; the dialog says how many. That only works with an empty content folder: when copying, the
example pages would overwrite notes of the same name, and QuartzHub never writes into a linked vault.
QuartzHub loads the basic template from GitHub, keeps it and asks again after a day. If it could not
be loaded, the dialog says so and offers Try again; without the template the project starts with
Quartz’s own defaults. The template can still be applied later
(5.9).
What happens on creating
Create project takes a minute or two. Meanwhile the bottom of the dialog says “Creating…”. In
that time QuartzHub

downloads Quartz from GitHub into the new folder, as a git repository with its whole history. The
connection to Quartz’s repository is cut afterwards, so a later push never lands there; updates
from Quartz still come (7.1);
installs the npm packages Quartz needs;
sets Quartz up with the answers from the dialog;
builds the site once, so that plugins which install something on their first build are ready the
next time;
applies the basic template, if chosen. The site’s language then becomes QuartzHub’s.

If one of the first three steps fails, the dialog stays open and says what did not work; the project
list then has nothing new. Otherwise the project is there: it is in the list, and its window opens.
If something went wrong with the template or there is something to report about it, the dialog says
so first and leads on with Go to the project. The project is usable in that case too.
What is in the folder

































quartz.config.yamlthe configuration: title, address, pluginscontent/the notes, a folder or a linkquartz/Quartz itself, with the stylesheets under quartz/styles/node_modules/the npm packages; large, but reinstallable at any time.quartz-gui/what QuartzHub keeps about the project: frames, snapshots, targets, bookspublic/the built site, new after every build
Everything except .quartz-gui/ is an ordinary Quartz project. What lives there is described in
8.2.

en/2-projects/03-opening-an-existing-pro.title: 2.3 – Opening an existing project
en/2-projects/03-opening-an-existing-pro.content:
Open existing project adds a folder in which Quartz is already set up to the project list. The
command is in the Projects window (the folder symbol in the toolbar), among the first steps of
the empty window, and in the menu as File ▸ Open Existing Project… (⌘O). The folder dialog starts
in the default project directory (2.5).
Which folder
The folder that holds quartz.config.yaml, not one above or below it. It is added and opened at
once; in the list the project is named after the folder.
If there is no quartz.config.yaml, QuartzHub still adds the folder to the list but does not open
it, and the row says Not a Quartz project. Remove from list… gets rid of such an entry; it
changes nothing about the folder.
If the folder is in the list already, no second entry appears; the existing project opens.
Where a project can come from
From a git repository. A project created on another Mac and pushed with Git Sync
(6.5) is fetched with git clone and then opened here. A fresh clone
lacks the npm packages, because node_modules/ does not travel; the Overview says so and fetches
them with Install (3.1). The downloaded plugins are missing as
well; Plugins ▸ Installed restores them from quartz.lock.json
(4.5).
Set up by hand. A Quartz cloned and set up following Quartz’s own instructions is a project like
any other to QuartzHub. Opening it changes nothing. Only when you set something does QuartzHub
write, and then into exactly the file you would have changed by hand.
A content folder that is a link
If content/ is a link to a vault, QuartzHub follows it. If the vault is on a volume that is not
mounted, or was moved, the Overview says so; the content folder can be linked again under
Configuration ▸ Site (4.2).

en/2-projects/04-duplicating-a-project.title: 2.4 – Duplicating a project
en/2-projects/04-duplicating-a-project.content:
A copy is a new project with the design of an existing one. What it is good for:

a second site with the same look, for another topic or another group;
a try without risk: an update, a new plugin, another layout, without touching the original.

Duplicate… is in the inspector of the Projects window when a project is selected, and in its
row’s context menu.

The Duplicate dialog. At the bottom it says what is not copied along.
Place, name and content

Where should the project live? and Name of the project folder as when creating
(2.2). The target folder must not exist yet, must not
lie inside the original, and the original must not lie inside it.
Content of the copy. The original’s content folder never comes along. The choices are:

Start empty (just a home page): a content folder with an index.md that carries the
project’s name and says where to link notes; without it the site would show a 404 page;
Link to a folder (an Obsidian vault, for instance): the content folder becomes a link, as
when creating;
Copy a folder in: the notes from the folder are taken over once.



What comes along and what stays

























Comes alongStays with the originalQuartz, the configuration including the base URL, the stylesheetsthe content folderthe installed pluginsthe snapshotsthe custom frames, theme presets and breakpointsset-aside content foldersthe git repository with its historythe publishing targets and what QuartzHub knows about earlier uploads
The targets stay behind for a good reason. A copy that inherited the original’s target would
overwrite its site at the first Publish now. The copy gets targets of its own
(6.7). The connections, meaning passwords and tokens,
apply to all projects anyway.
The base URL comes along. If the copy is to live at another address, change it under
Configuration ▸ Site (4.1).
The git repository comes along without its connection to the outside. The history stays, so
updates from Quartz can still be merged; but a git push of the copy does not land in the
original’s repository. For Git Sync, connect it to one of its own
(6.5).
What happens on duplicating
The bottom of the dialog says “Copying…”. QuartzHub copies what comes along, sets up the content
and installs the npm packages afresh instead of copying node_modules/; that takes a while. Then the
copy is in the list, and its window opens. It builds the site at the first preview.
If something fails, the dialog stays open and gives the reason.

en/2-projects/05-the-settings.title: 2.5 – The settings
en/2-projects/05-the-settings.content:
The settings apply to QuartzHub as a whole, not to one project. QuartzHub ▸ Settings… (⌘,) opens
them in a window of their own with four tabs. What you change there applies at once; only the
default project directory and the connections have a button to save.
General

Appearance

Theme: System setting, Light or Dark. With “System setting” QuartzHub follows the
Mac.
Language: Follow system language, Deutsch or English. The language is QuartzHub’s
own, not the sites’; theirs is in their configuration (4.1).

Projects

Default project directory: where the folder dialogs start when you create, open or duplicate
a project. Select picks the folder and saves it at once; a typed path is saved with Save or
the Return key.

On quit
Running dev servers says what happens to previews still running when QuartzHub quits:

Ask: QuartzHub asks every time. The question offers Cancel, Keep running and Stop
servers; with Don’t ask again the chosen answer becomes the setting.
Keep running: the servers keep running and stay reachable in the browser. At the next start
QuartzHub finds them again and asks whether they should keep running or stop.
Stop: the servers are stopped without asking.

Regardless of this, QuartzHub always asks at quit while an update, the restoring of a snapshot or a
publish is running: stopping halfway can leave the project half changed.
Connections
This holds the personal access token for GitHub and the connections to servers (SFTP, FTP) and
webhooks. They apply to all projects; which project publishes where is set in the project under
Publish. 6.7 describes both.
Runtime

Node runtime says what Quartz and npm run with:

In QuartzHub (the default): the Node QuartzHub brings. It is the same on every Mac and fits
Quartz.
From the system: the Node installed on the Mac. That only pays off when a package has to be
compiled during install and needs a particular Node for it. Quartz requires Node 22 or newer. Tools
such as nvm, fnm, asdf or mise pick the Node per folder, so the runtime can then differ from
project to project. If QuartzHub finds no Node on the Mac, it says so beforehand.

A change applies to everything started afterwards. A running preview keeps its Node until it is
restarted.
Below, it says which git QuartzHub uses. If the Mac has one installed, QuartzHub takes that one,
so your own setup (~/.gitconfig, credential helpers) keeps applying; otherwise the one it brings.
There is no switch for it.
Data & maintenance

Theme documentation: labels and descriptions of the options of community themes
(5.6), fetched from GitHub once and kept. Clear cache makes
QuartzHub load them afresh next time, say after a theme changed its options.
Storage location: the folder in which QuartzHub keeps the project list, the settings and the
connections, with Show in Finder. Normally that is
~/Library/Application Support/QuartzHub. The connections’ passwords and tokens are not there but
in the macOS keychain (8.2).

If QuartzHub could not read one of its own files at startup, say because it was killed while saving,
this tab says so at the top. The file was moved aside instead of overwritten; whatever it held is
missing from QuartzHub and has to be set up again.
At the very bottom are the versions of QuartzHub and macOS, for a bug report.

en/2-projects/index.title: 2 – Projects
en/2-projects/index.content:
A project is a folder holding a Quartz site: configuration, stylesheets, plugins and the content
folder with the notes. QuartzHub keeps a list of these folders; the folders themselves live wherever
you like.

The Projects window: the list, what its rows say and what
to do when a folder is missing.
Creating a new project: every question of the dialog
and what is in the folder afterwards.
Opening an existing project: a cloned
repository or a Quartz set up by hand.
Duplicating a project: what comes along, what stays
and why.
The settings: appearance, language, project folder, running
servers at quit, runtime.

en/3-overview/01-the-overview.title: 3.1 – The overview
en/3-overview/01-the-overview.content:
The overview of a project with nothing to do, freshly built.
At the top: needs attention, or “All good”
Above the cards stands one of the two:

Needs attention in orange, with the number of points. Each point says what is wrong, mostly
also why, and leads with a link to the page where it can be fixed.
“All good: content, git, CSS and configuration are fine.” in green.

If neither stands there, a check has not finished or could not run, say because the CSS could not
be checked. No “All good” then does not mean something is broken, only that QuartzHub does not know
(1.2).
These are the points the band can name:

With the “Fonts” plugin serving the fonts, the build fails without it ([[en/4-setup/01-websitenpm packages are missingQuartz does not build without them, as with a freshly cloned project. Running Run update once resolves it ([[en/7-maintenance/01-updates
The cards
Below the band are nine cards, in one to three columns depending on the window’s width. Each starts
with the one number or name it is about and ends with a link to the page that owns the topic.
Dev server. Whether the preview is running. If it is, its address stands there; a click opens it
in the browser. Below, since when it has been running, the WebSocket port it reloads through, and the
process number (PID); then the buttons Start or Stop and Restart. If the server exited
with an error, it says why here. → Preview & Build (6.1)
The site. Title, base URL and language of the site, and the content folder: “Own folder” with
the number of files, or the target of a link. “not set” and “target missing” stand out in colour. →
Configuration ▸ Site (4.1)
Git Sync. At the top right the branch. Below, how many commits are still to be pushed (↑) and
pulled (↓), how many changes are not committed yet, and the last commit with time and author. “no
remote branch” means: the project is not connected to any repository on the net. The card only reads
what git on the Mac knows; it does not go to the network for it. → Git Sync
(6.5)
Plugins. How many plugins are enabled and how many there are in all. → Plugins
(4.5)
Design. The active community theme or “Quartz default”, the number of own frames and
stylesheets, and whether the CSS compiles: CSS compiles, CSS error or CSS unchecked. →
Styles (5.5)
Build. When the site was last built, with the number and size of the files. The card looks at the
output folder for this; “Never built” means there is none. → Preview & Build
(6.2)
Publish. How many targets are set up, the first three with name and kind. → Publish
(6.7)
Updates. Whether there is something new for Quartz or the plugins: Core update available,
Plugin updates available, All up to date, Update unfinished or Cannot check. Below,
how many plugins were checked and how many checks failed. It is the only card that asks the network,
at GitHub; without a connection it says “Cannot check”, not “All up to date”. → Updates
(7.1)
Snapshots. How many there are, when the last one was taken and why, such as “Before config
change”. → Snapshots (7.2)
The toolbar
At the top right are three actions often needed from here:

Run build (hammer): builds the site once, like Project ▸ Run build (⌘B). When it is done,
the Build card says “Build finished.”; if it fails, it says the output is on Preview & Build.
Take snapshot: records the state of the project before you try something
(7.2).
Open project folder: shows the project folder in the Finder. The button is also in the
inspector, below the full path.

en/3-overview/index.title: 3 – Overview
en/3-overview/index.content:
Every project window opens on the Overview. It answers two questions: do I need to do
something? And how does the project stand right now? For anything further it leads to the page in
charge of it.

The overview: the “Needs attention” band, the nine cards and the
three actions in the toolbar.

en/4-setup/01-website.title: 4.1 – Site
en/4-setup/01-website.content:
Configuration ▸ Site edits the project’s quartz.config.yaml. At the top are the content folder
and the project image; they have chapters of their own (4.2,
4.3), because they save differently from the rest.

Configuration ▸ Site: content folder and project image at the top, the site settings below.
Saving
Everything below the project image is written to the file only by Save (⌘S). Before that,
QuartzHub takes a snapshot (“Before config change”), at most one every 15 minutes, so a series of
small changes does not fill the list. The file is changed rather than rewritten: comments and the
order of the keys stay.
Leaving the page with unsaved changes asks first
(1.3).
If the file cannot be read, say because it was broken by a hand edit, the page says so with the
reason and shows only the content folder. Fix the file in an editor, or get it back from a snapshot
(7.3).
Site settings

Site title: the name of the site. It appears in the browser tab, in the RSS feed and usually at
the top of the sidebar.
Title suffix: appended to every page’s title in the browser tab, such as “ · My notes”. It does
not appear on the page itself.
Base URL: the address of the finished site, without https://. Quartz builds links, the RSS
feed and preview images from it; with the “Fonts” plugin serving the fonts, the build fails without
it. For GitHub Pages it is usually name.github.io/repository
(6.8).
Site language: sets the site’s built-in texts such as “Search” or “Last modified”. The choices
are the language files the project ships; the texts themselves are changed under Translations
(4.4). For a site in several languages see
4.8.
Switch pages without reloading: a click on an internal link only swaps the content. That feels
faster; the site still works without JavaScript.
Link previews: hovering over an internal link shows a small window with the start of the target
page.
Prefetch pages (Quartz 5.1 and later): loads target pages before you click, so they appear at
once: Links on screen, When pointing at a link or Off.

Exclude notes and folders

Patterns (one per line): files and folders in the content folder that never get into the site,
such as private/** for a whole folder or *.excalidraw.md for a kind of file.
Publish files (Quartz 5.1 and later): All files in the content folder or Only those in
use. With “Only those in use”, pictures and other files only reach the site when a published page
uses them; the attachments of unpublished notes stay private.

What is in the content folder is public
Quartz publishes every note in the content folder that is neither excluded nor marked as a draft,
including notes nothing links to. Private notes belong in an excluded folder, or not in the content
folder at all.

Analytics
Embeds a provider’s counting script into every page. With No analytics, nothing is loaded and
nothing is measured.
Provider offers Plausible, Google, Umami, GoatCounter, PostHog, Tinylytics, Cabin, Clarity,
Matomo, Vercel and Rybbit. Depending on the provider, its fields appear below, named as Quartz names
them, such as websiteId or host; an asterisk means “required”. If a required field is missing, a
note says which; saving works anyway. Switching provider drops the old provider’s fields.
In many countries a counting script means the site has to tell its visitors about it. What applies
there is not this handbook’s subject.
Processing (Quartz 5.1 and later)
Since Quartz 5.1, Quartz does some things itself that used to need plugins: links, drafts, the
content index and frontmatter. Their settings are then in the configuration. These sections only
appear in a project with Quartz 5.1 or newer.
If the old plugin entries are still in the configuration, the Processing section says so.
Quartz keeps reading them. Move settings has Quartz move the settings into the configuration and
remove the old entries; QuartzHub takes a snapshot first. Unsaved changes have to be saved before.
Links

Resolve Markdown links: how a link of the form [text](path) finds its note: Shortest path
(as in Obsidian), Relative to the note or From the content folder.
Remove folders from link text: “folder/note” becomes “note”.
Open external links in a new tab, Icon after external links, Load images and videos only
when scrolled to.
Mark links to missing notes: such links get the CSS class broken.

Drafts

Publish drafts: pages with draft: true in their frontmatter are left off the site otherwise.

Content index, sitemap and RSS

Create the content index: without it, search, graph, sitemap and RSS are missing, and
QuartzHub cannot export documents (6.6).
Sitemap, RSS feed, the Items in the RSS feed, Whole page in the RSS feed (otherwise
only the description), Feed name (“index” gives index.xml) and Include pages without text.

Frontmatter

Delimiters: the characters above and below the frontmatter, usually ---.
Language: YAML or TOML.

If part of the processing is turned off in the configuration, its section is grey and says why.
At the very bottom the page points to Styles: colours and fonts are there
(5.5).

en/4-setup/02-the-content-folder.title: 4.2 – The content folder
en/4-setup/02-the-content-folder.content:
The content folder is content/ in the project folder: the Markdown notes Quartz builds the site
from. It is at the very top of Configuration ▸ Site. Unlike the rest of the page it is not part
of quartz.config.yaml; everything here applies at once, without Save.
Folder or link
The content folder is one of the two:

Real folder: the notes live in the project. Good when the site has a collection of its own.
Symbolic link: content/ points to a folder elsewhere, usually an Obsidian vault or a folder in
it. The notes stay where you write them, and every change shows in the preview at once.

The section shows which of the two applies, how many files are in it (hidden ones such as .obsidian
do not count) and the path, for a link also its target. If the target is gone, it says so in red,
and the overview reports “The content folder points nowhere”.
Publishing only part of a vault
The link need not point at the whole vault. A subfolder such as Vault/Public keeps everything else
safely out. Single notes and folders are excluded under Exclude notes and folders
(4.1).

Changing the source
Change source… opens the “Change content source” dialog:

New source folder: the folder with the notes, typed or picked with Select.
Strategy: Link makes content/ a link to the folder, Copy copies its contents once into
a real folder.

Apply then does three things:

It takes a snapshot (“Before content switch”). If that fails, nothing changes.
It sets the previous content folder aside instead of deleting it: a real folder is moved to
.quartz-gui/content-backups/; for a link, only where it pointed is recorded. A linked vault is
never touched.
It creates the new content folder, as a link or as a copy.

The source folder must not lie inside the content folder or contain it; the dialog says so if it
does.
Getting set-aside content folders back
Set-aside content folders are listed under Snapshots, in a list of their own
(7.3). Restore puts one of them back and sets the current one
aside as well. They can be deleted there too.
Set aside is not backed up
A set-aside real folder is the only copy of those notes; snapshots do not contain it. Deleting it
cannot be undone. Of a link only the target is recorded; the notes stay in the vault.

When the start page is missing
If there is no index.md at the top of the content folder, the site’s address shows a 404 page. The
section says so and offers Create start page…: the page gets the title you enter and, below it, a
list of the folders and notes at the top of the content folder right now. The list is not updated
later; the page is a beginning to write on yourself.
If the content folder is a link, the file is created in the linked folder, among your own notes; the
dialog says so beforehand. An existing index.md is never overwritten.
Content folder and git
To git, a link is only a reference. Taking the project to another Mac with Git Sync therefore
does not take the notes along; there the content folder has to be linked again. Whether snapshots
include the content folder is set under Snapshots; they never include a linked vault
(7.2).

en/4-setup/03-the-project-image.title: 4.3 – The project image
en/4-setup/03-the-project-image.content:
The project image is under Configuration ▸ Site, right below the content folder. It serves three
times:

in QuartzHub: in the project list and at the top of the project window’s sidebar;
as the site’s favicon, if the “favicon” plugin is enabled; the section says whether it is;
in the site header, if you switch that on.

Pictures are written at once, without Save and without a snapshot.
Choosing an image
Choose image… takes a PNG or JPEG file, ideally square. QuartzHub stores it as a PNG at
quartz/static/icon.png, scaled down to at most 512 pixels on the longer edge. The picture Quartz
brought there is kept the first time.
Remove image puts the original picture back; if there was none, there is none afterwards.
If it says “The site shows an image that was not chosen in QuartzHub”, the picture comes from a
template or was copied in by hand. One of your own replaces it.
Dark version
Image for dark mode… stores a second picture at quartz/static/icon-dark.png. It only applies
to the picture in the header while the site is shown dark; the favicon stays with the light one.
Remove dark image deletes the file at once.
Showing it in the header
Show in the site header puts the project image on top of every page as a link to the home page,
with the dark picture in dark mode. That works through the quartz-layout-box plugin. If it is
missing, QuartzHub asks when you switch this on whether to install it; for that it first saves the
page’s unsaved changes and needs a network connection. Afterwards the switch is on, but only Save
writes it to the configuration.
If a template’s layout box already shows the picture, such as the basic template’s, a note about
that stands in place of the switch.
Where exactly the picture sits in the header is moved on the stage under Layout ▸ Components
(5.3).

en/4-setup/04-translations.title: 4.4 – Translations
en/4-setup/04-translations.content:
For every language Quartz brings a file with the site’s built-in texts: “Search”, “Last modified”,
“Table of contents”, the titles of the callouts and so on. Configuration ▸ Translations edits
these files. Texts that plugins bring are not in them; those are set with the plugins, where they
allow it.

The texts of the German language file. Update protection at the top.
Changing texts

Language: the language file being edited. This only picks the file; which language the site
speaks is set under Site (4.1).
Search field: finds entries by key (such as components.search.title) or text.
Each entry shows its key and the text below. Entries marked JS are not plain text but a piece
of program code, for instance where a number is put into the text. They are saved verbatim as code;
changing them means writing valid TypeScript.

Save on this tab writes all changed entries of the chosen language; next to it, it says how many
are still unsaved; ⌘S does the same. An entry that could not be written keeps its change and says
why below.
Unsaved changes stay when you go to another page and come back. Choosing another language, closing
the window or quitting QuartzHub asks first: save, discard or cancel.
Saving does not take a snapshot. QuartzHub does keep the state before the first change of a language,
in .quartz-gui/locale-baseline/.
Update protection
The language files belong to Quartz. A core update (7.1) would
therefore overwrite your own wording with Quartz’s new texts. Update protection tells git to keep
your version of these files when in doubt. It is set up by itself at the first save; Enable now
sets it up right away.
The protection has a flip side: if an update changes a language file you changed yourself, your
version stays whole, and new texts from the update do not get in. If a text is missing afterwards,
add it here.

en/4-setup/05-plugins.title: 4.5 – Plugins
en/4-setup/05-plugins.content:
Almost everything Quartz does, a plugin does: reading Markdown, resolving links, search, the sidebar,
the table of contents. Plugins ▸ Installed shows all plugins of the project. The other tabs of
the page are editors for single plugins (4.6 to 4.9) and the marketplace (4.10).

Plugins ▸ Installed: your frames at the top, the visible components by position below.
The list
At the top, a search field and All, Active, Inactive filter the list; next to them it
says how many are active. The plugins stand in groups:

Your frames: the page grids from the layout editor. Quartz runs each one as a plugin; they are
set up under Layout ▸ Frames (5.4).
Visible components: what appears on the page, by position: Header, Left sidebar,
Right sidebar, Before the content, After the content, Footer and In the content.
Within a position by their priority.
Processing: what changes the notes behind the scenes, such as formatting, links, pictures, and
is not visible itself. First the Page types, then Transformers, filters & emitters, each in
the order Quartz applies them.
Maintenance: see below.

Each row shows the switch, the name, where the plugin comes from, a short description for known
plugins, and its place (position and priority, or order). Disabled plugins are paler. Marks may
be added:

Update available: there is a newer version (7.1).
Built into Quartz: since Quartz 5.1, Quartz does this itself; it is set up under
Configuration ▸ Site (4.1).
Error according to Quartz, Note from Quartz or intended: the result of Quartz’s own
check, see below.

Switching on and off, reordering, removing
A row’s switch writes to the configuration at once. The order is changed by dragging, with
Arrange ▸ Move Up and Move Down (⌥⌘↑, ⌥⌘↓) or in the context menu, each within a group;
QuartzHub renumbers the group (10, 20, 30 …). It does not work while a filter is active.
Remove is in the context menu. It asks, takes a snapshot and then has Quartz remove the plugin.
Your own frame is deleted from disk as well. The context menu also has Open repository on
GitHub.
The options
With a plugin selected, the inspector shows its settings. It saves without a button: switches
right away, text fields when you leave them or press Return. Every change takes a snapshot, at most
one every 15 minutes.

At the top name, source, description and Plugin enabled.
Placement (visible components only): position, priority, display (all devices, mobile
only, desktop only), condition (such as not-index, has-tags, has-backlinks, has-toc) and
group with its options. The mouse does the same on the stage: Show on the stage leads to
Layout ▸ Components (5.3).
Options: a form made from what the plugin says about its options. Yes/no becomes a switch, a
choice a menu, lists get buttons to add and reorder. From eight options on there is a search field;
rarely used ones are under Rarely needed.

About the fields:

changed means: the value is in the configuration. The button next to it removes it again, and
the plugin takes its default.
no effect means: the option only applies together with another one that is set differently
right now.
What QuartzHub cannot show as a form is edited as JSON. Invalid JSON is not saved.
Values that are in the configuration but that the plugin does not describe are under Unknown
keys.
If a plugin does not describe its options at all, the fields come from its defaults, and Add
another option takes a key with a value.

QuartzHub reads the description of the options from the plugin’s package, without running it.
Quartz’s own check (Quartz 5.1 and later)
From Quartz 5.1 on, QuartzHub runs quartz plugin doctor, Quartz’s own check of the plugins, after
every change. What it reports appears as a mark on the row and in the inspector under Quartz
reports, in Quartz’s words. “intended” means: Quartz objects to something QuartzHub does on
purpose, such as several entries of the same plugin, one per box or navigation.
If GitHub Markdown and Obsidian Markdown run in the wrong order, a note above the list says so;
Swap the order fixes it.
Maintenance
At the very bottom are two buttons that work on the downloaded plugins in .quartz/plugins/:

Restore from quartz.lock.json downloads every plugin in the version quartz.lock.json records.
That is needed after cloning on another Mac
(2.3); missing npm packages are installed first.
Remove orphaned plugin folders deletes downloaded plugins the configuration no longer points
to.

Neither changes the configuration.

en/4-setup/06-navigations.title: 4.6 – Navigations
en/4-setup/06-navigations.content:
Plugins ▸ Navigations sets up the quartz-navigations plugin. It builds navigations from the
folders and notes of the content folder: a tree list in the sidebar, a menu in the header, a sitemap
in the footer, previous and next below the text. Each navigation is an entry of its own of the
plugin; a site can have several.
If the plugin is not installed, the tab says so; it is installed in the marketplace via
boxi-os/quartz-navigations (4.10).

The project’s navigations at the top, the preview below, the inspector on the right.
How the editor tabs are built
Navigations, Additional content, Languages and Forms are built the same way:

The list of entries at the top, the preview of the site below. The grip between them
can be dragged (1.3).
The inspector on the right with the settings of the selected entry.
Saving is immediate: switches when flipped, text fields when you leave them. Every change takes
a snapshot, at most one every 15 minutes. ⌘S does not apply here.
The preview shows the site through the dev server; if it is not running, Start preview
starts it. At the top you choose the page and the width (Desktop, Tablet, Mobile). The
selected entry is marked in the preview, and below it says whether it occurs on this page. Zoom
onto element enlarges it. After a change the preview reloads as soon as Quartz has rebuilt.
Show on the stage leads to Layout ▸ Components, where the place on the page is moved
(5.3). All options leads to the entry under Installed,
with the general form (4.5).
If the editor does not know the installed version of the plugin, a note says that details may
differ.

Creating a navigation
➕ New navigation in the toolbar asks for the variant. The navigation goes where that variant
usually stands; it can be moved on the stage afterwards.




























































VariantWhat it isPlaced firstTreeNested list, all openLeft sidebarAccordionFolders fold open, the path to the page is openLeft sidebarSide panelsFolders open a panel beside themLeft sidebarSelect listA jump menu, folders as groupsLeft sidebarBarFirst level in one lineHeaderDropdownA line, folders open a panel belowHeaderMega menuPanel with the second level as columnsHeaderTabsFirst level as tabs, children in a second lineHeaderColumnsHeadings with children below, a sitemapFooterPrevious / nextPrevious and next pageAfter the content
The list
Each row shows name, variant and position, disabled ones with “off”. A row’s buttons duplicate
the navigation or remove it; the last one cannot be removed. Removing deletes the entry with all
its options from the configuration; the plugin stays installed.
Setting up
For the selected navigation the inspector shows:

Navigation active: switches it on or off without deleting it.
Variant: the same ten tiles as when creating; a click changes the variant, the other settings
stay.
Options: the settings of the chosen variant first, then the general ones. Options that have no
effect with this variant are grey and say why, such as “Only applies with the variant …”. Some
variants behave differently on a phone; what applies there is set by an option of its own.

What each option does, the plugin describes next to the field.

en/4-setup/07-additional-content.title: 4.7 – Additional content
en/4-setup/07-additional-content.content:
Plugins ▸ Additional content sets up the quartz-layout-box plugin. A box is a piece of content of
your own that stands in the same place on every page: a note in the sidebar, an imprint link in the
footer, a logo in the header. Each box is an entry of its own of the plugin. The tab works like the
other editors (4.6).

The boxes at the top, the files in the middle, the preview below.
Creating and managing boxes
➕ New box creates a box with a sample text in the left sidebar at once. Each row of the list
shows name, kind of content and position, plus “desktop only” or “mobile only” where set. A row’s
buttons duplicate or remove the box. Removing only deletes the entry; a file the box shows stays.
The content of a box
In the inspector, Content chooses where the box takes its content from:

Text in the configuration: HTML, written right in the inspector. Good for short things.
File: a Markdown or HTML file under quartz/static/. Good for longer things, and the file can
be edited with any editor.

Switching from text to file asks whether to remove the text from the configuration; afterwards it is
gone. A box can also have content of its own per language and page, which then takes precedence.
Below are the plugin’s other options, such as heading, appearance and languages.
Files
The middle pane manages the files that boxes use:

Snippets in quartz/static/snippets/: New file creates a Markdown or HTML file, Add file
copies an existing one in. Each file says which boxes use it. Renaming a file updates the boxes that
name it. Deleting moves it to the trash.
Pictures in quartz/static/images/: Add picture takes PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG and AVIF.
If a picture a box uses is renamed, QuartzHub does not change the references in the text; that is
up to you.
Project image: icon.png and icon-dark.png, for looking only. In a snippet you include it with
the path shown there (4.3).

Editing snippets
The pencil on a snippet opens it in the code editor, with line numbers and colours for HTML and
Markdown. The snippet is a file of its own: Save snippet writes it, not the box’s options and not
⌘S.
Available placeholders insert values at build time, in the text as in the box’s title:





































PlaceholderBecomes{{title}}title of the page, from its frontmatter{{slug}}path of the page, such as “folder/note”{{root}}way to the home page, for links and pictures: {{root}}/static/images/logo.png{{siteTitle}}title of the site{{baseUrl}}address of the site{{locale}}, {{lang}}language of the page, such as “en-US” or just “en”{{frontmatter.author}}any entry in the page’s frontmatter
A click inserts the placeholder at the cursor. An unknown one stays as written.
Insert image… copies a picture to quartz/static/images/ and inserts the reference. An SVG file
can also be inserted as code; QuartzHub then removes whatever in it could run program code, and says
what it removed.

en/4-setup/08-languages.title: 4.8 – Languages
en/4-setup/08-languages.content:
Plugins ▸ Languages sets up the quartz-multilanguage plugin. It turns one content folder into a
site in several languages: it detects which language a note is written in, connects translations of
the same page, puts a language switcher on the page and tells search engines which version is meant
for which language. The plugin applies to the whole site, not per entry. The tab works like the
other editors (4.6).
This handbook is built that way: the German pages at the top of the content folder, the English ones
in the folder en/, connected through a shared key in the frontmatter.

Two languages, German as the default. The settings below them, the preview at the bottom.
Switching on and off
The On switch at the top builds the site with or without language detection, switcher and
redirects. The settings are kept.
Languages
➕ New language asks for the code with which folders, file names and frontmatter name the
language, such as fr. The list shows each language with code, name and locale; Default marks
the default language, “not published” one whose pages do not reach the site. The languages stand in
the switcher in this order; reorder by dragging, with Arrange ▸ Move Up/Move Down (⌥⌘↑, ⌥⌘↓)
or in the inspector with Earlier and Later.
For a selected language the inspector shows:

code, label, native and locale. A new code does not change folder or file names in
the content folder; default language and publishing follow along.
Default language: applies to pages that detection assigns to no language. It can only be handed
over by making another language the default.
Publish: switched off, the site is built without this language’s pages, for a translation that
is not finished yet, say. The last published language stays on.

Removing a language takes it out of the configuration. Its pages stay and count as pages of the
default language afterwards.
Settings
Below the languages are the groups of settings, each with a summary such as “Detection: folder,
suffix, frontmatter”. A click shows the group in the inspector. Which groups there are is up to the
plugin; usually they are:

Detection: how the plugin tells a note’s language: by folder (en/…), by a suffix in the file
name (note.en.md) or by the frontmatter.
Language switcher: how it looks and what it shows. Where it stands is set on the stage (Show
on the stage).
Addresses (SEO): what search engines are told about which version of a page is meant for which
language.

What each option does, the plugin describes next to the field.
Built-in texts per language
The site’s built-in texts such as “Search” come from Quartz’s language files for every language;
they can be changed under Translations (4.4).

en/4-setup/09-forms.title: 4.9 – Forms
en/4-setup/09-forms.content:
A site made by Quartz is a collection of fixed files; it cannot take a message itself. The
quartz-forms plugin therefore builds forms that send their message to a service which passes it on:
an endpoint of your own, a provider such as Formspree or Web3Forms, or the relay, a small PHP
script on your own web space. Plugins ▸ Forms sets all of this up.
If the plugin is not installed, the tab says so; it is installed in the marketplace via
boxi-os/quartz-forms (4.10). The basic template brings it along,
with a contact form that sends nothing yet. The tab works like the other editors
(4.6).

At the top the forms and the settings for all of them, below the preview. “Demo” means the form
sends nothing.
Creating a form
➕ New form asks what to Start with:





























TemplateFieldsContactname, e-mail, message, consentFeedbackrating and comment on the pageSign-upname, e-mail, date, peopleSurveyanonymous: choice, scale, commentEmptyone message field, the rest is yours
Then the Id, such as contact: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. A page embeds the form
with it.
Embedding a form
A form appears in one of two ways:


On a page that names it by its id, in one of three ways:

in the frontmatter: form: contact, for several form: [contact, feedback];
as a placeholder in the text: {{form:contact}};
as a code block of the language quartz-form with the id as its content.

The frontmatter key and the code block’s language can be changed under Settings for all forms ▸
Technical.


As the layout form in the same place on every page, below the text for instance. A page hides
it with form: false in its frontmatter.


The list says for each form on how many pages it stands. If a page names a form that does not exist,
it says so above the list, because the build stops on it. The preview jumps to a page that embeds the
selected form.
The list and the check
Each form shows title and id, fields, way of sending, encryption and the number of pages, plus marks
such as Layout or anonymous. Copying creates a copy with the id …-copy; removing first says
which pages embed the form, because they no longer build afterwards.
After every change QuartzHub has the plugin check its forms. Above the list it says that quartz-forms
reports no problems, or the number of problems; a problem stops the build. The messages also appear
with the form and the group they concern.
Setting up a form
In the inspector, the parts of a form fold open, General and Fields first. Changing the id
asks first when pages use it; they then have to be changed too.

The “Contact” form chosen: its fields on the right, the first one open; the preview shows a page that
embeds it.
Settings for all forms
Below the forms are the shared groups. Each form can change single values for itself.

Sending: where the forms send to: the Relay, an Endpoint of your own, Formspree,
Web3Forms, the visitor’s Mail program or Demo (sends nothing).
Keys: public PGP keys that encrypting forms send to. A key comes from a file, which is copied to
quartz-forms/keys/ in the project, or is pasted. QuartzHub does not accept private keys.
Spam protection: traps for bots, a time trap, a puzzle, a captcha provider and a limit per hour.
A captcha’s secret key is entered with the relay.
Layout form: which form stands on every page, and where.
Texts: the plugin’s wording, such as error messages, replaceable per language. The plugin’s
wording stands in grey; Plugin wording resets your own text.
Technical: how the plugin recognises an embedding.
Relay: only when a form sends through the relay; see below.

The relay
The relay is a PHP script (send.php with its configuration) that passes the forms’ messages on as
mail. It lives on your own web space, so it needs a web space with PHP. QuartzHub has the plugin
generate it and uploads it through one of the project’s targets.
What the relay needs:

Target: a publishing target of the project of the type SFTP, FTP or folder
(6.7). The relay goes into a Folder below its
path, such as forms, and never deletes anything there. If the site target transfers with rsync and
deletes what the build lacks, QuartzHub offers to exclude the folder there.
Address of send.php: where the forms send to. Use the suggestion builds it from base URL and
folder.
Sender: an address of the web space’s domain, or mail servers reject the messages.
Recipients: the forms name recipients by name, such as “contact”; here each name gets its
address.
Captcha secret, if a form uses a captcha.

Optional: Allowed origins (the relay only accepts requests from these addresses), Sending the
mails through PHP mail() or sendmail, and under Rarely needed a subject prefix, a folder for
counters and a new secret.
Upload relay uploads it and then asks by itself whether it answers; this probe sends no mail. The
answer appears below, such as “The relay answers at …”, or what is wrong: no PHP, a redirect, a
refused origin, an unreadable configuration. At the top of the group it says whether the relay was
changed since the upload. Save as folder … writes it to a folder, for a web space you fill some
other way; Remove from server … takes it down again.
Where the addresses live
QuartzHub keeps the relay’s recipient addresses and secrets in the keychain, never in the project
folder and never on the site. On another Mac they are therefore missing; the group says so, and you
enter them again. Removing the project from the list deletes them
(2.1). In the uploaded config.php and in a saved folder
they stand in plain text.

en/4-setup/10-marketplace.title: 4.10 – Marketplace
en/4-setup/10-marketplace.content:
Plugins ▸ Marketplace shows the catalogue of the
quartz-community on GitHub: Quartz’s own plugins and other
people’s.

The marketplace, sorted by stars. Installed plugins are marked.
The catalogue
QuartzHub loads the catalogue from GitHub the first time the tab is opened and keeps it for a quarter
of an hour. Reload catalog in the toolbar fetches it again at once.
Each row shows name, description, stars and, where it applies, Installed or Archived. At the
top are the repositories that declare themselves a Quartz plugin, sorted by stars. Everything else of
the quartz-community, such as Quartz itself, libraries and templates, is folded below; most of it is
not a plugin. The search field searches name and description.
Without signing in, GitHub only answers a limited number of requests per hour. If that is used up or
GitHub does not answer, the tab says so, and below is only a placeholder. A personal access token
for GitHub raises the limit; QuartzHub uses the one from the settings
(2.5).
Looking at a plugin
With a plugin selected, the inspector shows its description from the repository (the README), a link
to GitHub and Install. Pictures in the README only appear as text there; GitHub shows them in
full.
Installing
Install takes a snapshot and then has Quartz add the plugin: Quartz downloads it, enters it in
quartz.config.yaml and records the version in quartz.lock.json. Afterwards it is under
Installed, with its defaults. This needs a network connection.
Add a plugin from GitHub installs a plugin that is not in the catalogue. Enter
github:owner/repository and press Add. QuartzHub passes the text to Quartz unchanged; what else
Quartz accepts is described in the Quartz documentation.
Plugins are programs
A plugin runs at every build with the rights of your account. Only install what comes from a source
you trust.

en/4-setup/index.title: 4 – Setup
en/4-setup/index.content:
The Setup group in the sidebar has two pages. Configuration sets what the site is: title,
address, language, where the notes come from. Plugins sets what Quartz does with the notes and
what appears on the pages.
Configuration

Site: title, address, language, exclusions, analytics and the
processing of Quartz 5.1.
The content folder: a real folder or a link to a vault, and
how to switch without losing anything.
The project image: favicon, picture in the header, light and
dark version.
Translations: the site’s built-in texts, such as “Search”.

Plugins

Plugins: the installed plugins, their order and their options.
Navigations: menus, accordions, previous and next.
Additional content: boxes of your own with text, HTML or
pictures.
Languages: one site in several languages.
Forms: contact forms and how their messages arrive.
Marketplace: finding and installing new plugins.

en/5-design/01-the-layers.title: 5.1 – The layers
en/5-design/01-the-layers.content:
The look of a Quartz site comes from several layers lying on top of each other. What lies higher
wins. The four tabs under Styles are these layers, in this order:






























LayerWhereWhat it sets1. BasicsStyles ▸ Basicsthe base colours for light and dark and the three fonts, from the configuration2. Community themeStyles ▸ Community themesa ready-made colour scheme; overrides the basics3. VariablesStyles ▸ Variablessingle CSS variables; beat the theme4. Custom CSSStyles ▸ Custom CSSrules of your own, for everything the other layers cannot do
The inspector on the right shows the same order, plus whether a theme is active and how many
variables are overridden.
What follows from it
With a community theme active, many basic colours have no effect. Styles ▸ Basics shows this:
at the top it says how many colours and fonts the theme overrides, and those fields are paler. They
apply again once the theme is off.
Against a theme, a colour is changed under Variables. The values there win, even where the theme
sets the same variable. The exception are colours a theme sets for one kind of element only, such as
callouts; those are changed in custom CSS.
Custom CSS is the last resort, not the first. A colour that exists as a variable is better changed
under Variables: it then applies everywhere the variable is used, separately for light and dark.
Within custom CSS
Quartz only includes one file, quartz/styles/custom.scss. That file loads everything else, in the
order listed under Custom CSS on the right under Load order:

your own stylesheets in quartz/styles/custom/ and imported/, in their order;
_quartzcontrol.scss: the fonts and variables QuartzHub writes;
custom.scss itself, always last.

What loads later wins among equally specific rules. A rule in custom.scss therefore beats a value
under Variables; the Variables tab warns when custom.scss sets the same variable. A file under
custom/, however, loads before the variables and loses to them.
Why the variables beat the theme
Quartz and the themes put their rules into CSS layers (@layer). What a project writes itself is in
no layer, and a rule outside all layers beats every rule inside one, however specific it is.

And the layout?
The layout is none of these layers. It sets which components stand where and what the page’s grid
looks like (5.2); the styles set how it looks.

en/5-design/02-layout-overview.title: 5.2 – Layout overview
en/5-design/02-layout-overview.content:
Three terms
Components are the visible parts of a page: search, table of contents, graph, a navigation, a
box. Each is a plugin entry (4.5) with a position: header, left or
right sidebar, before or after the content, footer. Components are placed once for all pages.
Page types are the kinds of page Quartz builds: content pages (the notes), folder pages, tag
pages, the 404 page and, depending on the plugins, more such as Bases or Canvas pages. Each page type
can differ from the rest: hide components, clear areas, use a frame of its own.
A frame is the grid of a page: which areas there are, where they lie and how wide they are.
Quartz brings Standard, Full width and Minimal; your own are built under Frames
(5.4).
Layout has three tabs for this: Overview shows everything, Components is the stage for
moving things, Frames the editor for grids of your own.
Saving
Overview and Components change quartz.config.yaml, Frames changes a frame. Both are written only by
Save (⌘S), each for the tab in front. Before the configuration is saved, QuartzHub takes a
snapshot, at most one every 15 minutes. Leaving the page with unsaved changes asks first.
The overview

The overview: the figures at the top, the table below.
The overview changes nothing; it shows and leads on. A click on a component, a page type or one of
your own frames opens the place where it is set.
The figures at the top each open a list below:

components placed, split into always, desktop only, mobile only;
with a condition: components that only appear on some pages, say only with a table of contents;
switched off: components in the tray that are not built;
page types, and how many of them differ, with what is hidden or cleared in each;
own frames, and which are assigned to no page type.

The table “Where each component appears” has a column per page type and a row per component,
grouped by position. The first row shows each page type’s frame; a dot at a page type means it
differs from “All pages”. Each cell says whether the component gets there:

appears, or only on certain widths;
hidden on this page type, or its area cleared;
its area is not assigned in this frame or shown at no width;
unknown, when the frame comes from a plugin and QuartzHub does not know its structure.

A cell’s tooltip gives the exact reason. The legend is below the table.

en/5-design/03-layout-components.title: 5.3 – Components
en/5-design/03-layout-components.content:
Layout ▸ Components shows the page in miniature, drawn in the frame of the chosen page type: the
tray of components at the top, the stage with its areas below, the flex groups at the
bottom. Everything here goes into a draft; only Save (⌘S) writes the configuration
(5.2).

The stage for all pages in the desktop view. The summary per position on the right.
The head

Page type: All pages or a single page type. A customized one reads “(customized)”.
View: Desktop, Tablet or Mobile. With a frame of your own, the widths are shown.
Frame (only for a page type): Standard, Full width, Minimal, one of your own frames, or the one
the page type’s plugin brings.
Left/Right sidebar (Quartz 5.1 and later): what the sidebar does when its content is taller
than the screen: Screen height (the single components scroll), Scrolls itself or Scrolls
with the page. This only works in Quartz’s standard frame.
Edit frame opens one of your own frames in the editor. Remove customization resets a page
type to “All pages”.

What applies to all and what to one page type
With a page type chosen, only hiding and clearing apply to it. What you move or set in the
inspector applies to all pages.

Moving

Dragging onto another component puts the dragged one before it; onto the free rest of an area,
at the end.
Dragging from the tray inserts another instance, a second navigation for instance. A switched-off
component is switched back on on the way.
Dragging into the tray switches a component off; a duplicate is removed.
With the keyboard, the inspector does the same: Position, Earlier and Later.

QuartzHub renumbers the components of a position as it goes (10, 20, 30 …), so their order in the
configuration matches the stage. A click into empty space or Esc clears the selection.
Clearing (the eraser on an area, only for a page type) leaves an area empty on that page type; a
second click fills it again.
Dashed components are not on the page shown; the tooltip says why.
The inspector
For a selected component:

Hide on {page type} (only for a page type). If there are several instances of the same
component, this hides all of them; Quartz cannot exclude single duplicates separately.
Position, Order with Earlier and Later.
Visibility: Always, Desktop only or Mobile only. “Desktop only” applies on the tablet
too; Quartz only switches at the mobile boundary.
Condition: Always, Not on the home page, Only on pages with tags, … with
backlinks, … with a table of contents, or a custom one a plugin brings.
Group and, inside a group, how the component takes up room in it.
Duplicate, Put in the tray or Remove duplicate.
Options: the same form as under Plugins ▸ Installed.

Without a selection, the inspector shows a Summary: the frame and, per position, its components.
Flex groups
Components of the same group stand side by side or one below the other instead of each on its own
line, such as search, the light/dark switch and the language switcher in one line in the header. Per
group you set Arrangement (side by side, stacked, each also reversed), Wrapping, Gap and
Priority. A new group is created at the bottom with a name and Add; a component joins it via
Group in the inspector or by dragging it into the group.

en/5-design/04-layout-frames.title: 5.4 – Frames
en/5-design/04-layout-frames.content:
A frame is the grid of a page: which areas there are (header, sidebars, content, footer), where they
lie and how wide they are. What appears in the areas is set under Components; that is also where
the frame per page type is chosen (5.3).
Layout ▸ Frames builds frames of your own without writing CSS. Each frame is set up separately
for desktop, tablet and mobile.

One of your own frames in the desktop view. The grid’s settings on the right.
Choosing and creating frames
At the top, Frame chooses between Quartz standard (view only) and your own frames,
Breakpoint between desktop, tablet and mobile. The toolbar has:

➕ New frame: an empty frame with all areas, none placed yet;
Duplicate: a copy of the chosen frame, “…-kopie”;
Delete: page types that use it fall back to the standard frame;
Save (⌘S): writes the frame.

On Quartz standard the tab shows how Quartz divides a page without a frame of your own.
Customize as your own frame creates a copy of it, Create an empty frame an empty one.
The grid
Above the grid are the areas not on this grid. + Add area creates a new one.

Dragging an area onto a free cell places it; back into the list takes it off the grid, on this
breakpoint only. A shadow shows where it would land; red means it would cover another area.
At the edges of a selected area you drag its spans across several rows or columns.
A click shows its settings in the inspector. A click into empty space or Esc clears the
selection.

Below the grid are warnings, for instance when areas overlap, reach past the grid, a position is
assigned to no area (its components then do not appear in this frame), or an area is visible at no
breakpoint.
The inspector
Without a selection it sets up the frame:

Frame name.
Grid for {breakpoint}: Rows and Columns (1 to 12), Row gap and Column gap.
Width and padding: Maximum width, Alignment and the paddings. Without a maximum width
the frame uses the whole window width.
Column widths (empty = equal shares) and Row heights (empty = as tall as the content), as
CSS values such as 16rem or 1fr.
Named grid lines, if you want to address the lines in custom CSS later.
Copy to {breakpoint}: takes over this breakpoint’s whole grid onto another, without asking.

With an area it sets up that area:
