Area name: becomes a CSS-safe name of lower-case letters, digits and hyphens; when that differs
from what was typed, the name it is saved as is shown below.
Slot: which position the area shows, or none.
Area of its own: the area then only shows the components dragged here under Components, not
everything belonging to its position. That way a position gets two areas, a sidebar at the top and
at the bottom for instance.
Row span, Column span and Visible on {breakpoint}.
Move to row and column: the same as dragging, with the keyboard.
Remove from grid (this breakpoint only) and Remove area.

Breakpoints
Breakpoints sets from which window width your own frames switch to tablet and mobile. The
default is 1200 and 800 pixels, as in Quartz. This section’s own Save writes at once and applies
to all your own frames. Quartz’s built-in frames and community themes bring their own values.
What happens on saving
To Quartz, a frame of your own is a plugin: a folder under .quartz-gui/authored-frames/ with the
description of the grid and the generated CSS. A new frame is registered with Quartz at its first
save, after QuartzHub takes a snapshot. Before every build and every start of the preview, QuartzHub
rewrites all frames.
With the preview running, a change to an existing frame only shows after a restart; the tab offers
Restart dev server.
Page types name their frame by its name. When a frame is renamed, saving it updates the page types
that use it.
Your own frames do not travel with git (3.1).

en/5-design/05-styles-basics.title: 5.5 – Styles ▸ Basics
en/5-design/05-styles-basics.content:
Styles ▸ Basics is the bottom layer (5.1): the colours and fonts
written in quartz.config.yaml.

Fonts, font delivery and the colours for light mode.
Saving
The four tabs under Styles share one Save (⌘S): what you change on one tab survives switching
to another and is saved together with it. Before the configuration is written, QuartzHub takes a
snapshot, at most one every 15 minutes. Some things apply at once, without saving; it says so where
they are.
With a theme active
If a community theme is active, a note at the top says how many colours and fonts it overrides. Those
fields are paler; they can still be changed and apply once the theme is off. Against the theme,
values are changed under Variables (5.7).
Fonts

Font source: Google Fonts or Your own local font. With Google the fields offer every
Google font; typing filters. Locally nothing is loaded; the font has to be in the project, via
Import a custom font for instance.
Font (Headings), (Body text) and (Code): the font for headings, text and code.

Below a field it says when something is wrong: Google does not know the name or spells it
differently, the theme overrides the font, or a variable in the project does; then the field changes
nothing on the site.
Font delivery
Where the fonts come from for visitors is a question of privacy: if the site loads them from Google,
Google learns about every visit.

Serve fonts locally (no Google request on visit): on saving, QuartzHub fetches the font files
from Google once and stores them in quartz/static/fonts/. The site then makes no request to Google.
Switched off, saving removes the local copies again.
Above, it says who loads fonts in the project right now: Quartz itself, QuartzHub, the “Fonts”
plugin or the theme. What links Google directly is shown in orange.
Fetch into the project now saves the page at once and fetches the fonts.
Load the theme’s own fonts (only with a theme): a theme loads its fonts from unpkg.com;
QuartzHub cannot serve them locally. Switched off, your own fonts apply.

If the “Fonts” plugin serves the fonts itself, it needs a base URL (4.1).
Known conflicts
With the “Fonts” plugin and a theme together, the headings do not follow the theme. Add fix at
once creates a small file custom/fix-heading-fonts.scss that fixes it; afterwards it is listed under
Custom CSS like any other.
Import a custom font
Choose file… takes a .ttf, .otf, .woff or .woff2 file, copies it to quartz/static/fonts/
at once and writes the matching @font-face rule. Use directly for sets it as the font for
headings, text or code right away; that applies after saving.
Unused fonts lists imported fonts nothing uses. Removing deletes rules and files at once, without
a snapshot.
Colours
Per mode, light and dark, the base colours with their names from Quartz:













































NameWhat Quartz uses it forlightbackgroundlightgraylines and bordersgrayheavier borders, links in the graphdarkgraybody textdarkheadings and iconssecondarylinks, the current page in the graphtertiaryhover, visited pages in the graphhighlightbackground of internal linkstextHighlighthighlighted text (==like this==)
Each has a colour well and a text field for any CSS colour value. What a theme overrides carries the
mark THEME.

en/5-design/06-community-themes.title: 5.6 – Community themes
en/5-design/06-community-themes.content:
Community themes are ready-made colour schemes, many of them after themes for Obsidian. They come
through the @quartz-themes/core plugin and lie on top of the basics
(5.1).

A switched-off theme, two presets and the catalogue.
Choosing a theme
Catalog lists the themes by their stars on GitHub; the search field filters, for “tokyo-night”,
“catppuccin” or “nord” for instance. A click shows a theme in the inspector: description, modes,
variants, whether it lets you adjust its colours. Install & activate installs it at once and sets
it in the draft; only Save writes it to the configuration.
The list comes from npm and is kept for a quarter of an hour; without a network only a few known
themes stand there as placeholders.
The current theme
At the top it says which theme is active. Disable community themes switches it off and keeps its
settings; Turn back on switches it on. Without a theme, the colours and fonts from Basics
apply.
The theme’s settings
Many themes bring settings of their own, such as an accent colour or the style of headings. QuartzHub
shows them with labels and descriptions from the original theme, in groups and with a search field;
Reset on an option takes it back. QuartzHub fetches the descriptions from GitHub once and keeps
them; Reload docs fetches them again, Settings ▸ Data & maintenance clears all of them
(2.5). Without descriptions, only the raw switches are shown.
What a theme does not offer as a setting is changed under Variables.
Presets
Save as preset saves the current theme with its settings under a name, at once, in
.quartz-gui/theme-presets.json. My presets lists them; Apply installs the preset’s theme and
takes its settings into the draft. A deleted preset is gone.
Themes load fonts from outside
A theme loads its fonts from unpkg.com. If you do not want that, switch off the theme’s own fonts
under Basics ▸ Font delivery (5.5).

en/5-design/07-variables.title: 5.7 – Variables
en/5-design/07-variables.content:
Almost every colour and font and many spacings of a Quartz site come from CSS variables such as
--secondary or --bodyFont. Styles ▸ Variables shows them all, says where each gets its value
and who uses it, and changes them precisely. Values here beat the theme
(5.1).

The main variables, the base colours unfolded. On the right, which ones are changed.
The list

Main variables: the variables Quartz derives from the base colours, in groups such as base
colours, surfaces, text, navigation, fonts. A group shows how many in it are changed.
All theme and build variables: everything the theme, plugins or the last build bring. QuartzHub
only knows the total after a build. A search field (such as “callout”, “h1”, “background”),
Changed only, a filter for colours and other values and Reload help to find them.

Each row shows the colour for light and dark, the name, the value, how many other variables depend
on it, and where it comes from: changed, own variable or community theme.
Looking at a variable
A click shows the variable in the inspector:

Current value, for light and dark, with the colour value.
Source: Quartz, the theme, a stylesheet or the last build, with the chain the value comes
through, in the form --a → --b → value.
Uses these variables and Used by these variables: a click jumps there. Below, it says how
many further variables a change affects.

Changing a variable
Under Your own value you enter the new value, for colours also through a colour well. Different
in dark mode separates light and dark. Reset to original value takes the change back. A
variable that only exists in your own project can be removed; every place using it then has no value.
Saving is Save (⌘S). QuartzHub writes the values into a section of its own in
quartz/styles/_quartzcontrol.scss. A value must not contain a semicolon, a curly brace, a backslash
or a comment; otherwise QuartzHub saves nothing at all and says which value it is.
Better the source than what derives from it
Many variables derive from a few. Changing --secondary changes all links, highlights and whatever
depends on them. The line “Your own value here affects … other variables” shows how far a change
reaches.

If custom.scss sets the same variable itself, it wins there; a note at the top says so.

en/5-design/08-custom-css.title: 5.8 – Custom CSS
en/5-design/08-custom-css.content:
Styles ▸ Custom CSS is the top layer (5.1): rules of your own in SCSS
or CSS, for everything basics, theme and variables cannot do.

custom.scss in the editor, the load order of the stylesheets on the right.
The files
Quartz only includes quartz/styles/custom.scss; that file loads all the others. The inspector on
the right shows the order under Load order: first your own stylesheets in quartz/styles/custom/
and imported/, then _quartzcontrol.scss, last custom.scss itself. Files loaded later override
earlier ones.

New file creates a stylesheet under custom/ and appends it to the order.
Import file… (toolbar) copies a .scss or .css file into imported/. If a file of the same name
is there, QuartzHub asks whether to replace it.
Per file: Move Up, Move Down, Rename, Delete. These file actions apply at once,
without a snapshot.
Present, but not loaded lists files that lie in the folders but are not loaded; Load it takes
them in.

A click on a name opens the file in the editor, in a tab. Changes to the text are written by Save
(⌘S).
_quartzcontrol.scss belongs to QuartzHub
What stands between the markers in _quartzcontrol.scss, QuartzHub rewrites at every change to the
order, fonts or variables. Text outside the markers stays, but rules of your own belong in a file of
their own.

The editor
A code editor with line numbers, colours for SCSS and CSS and the macOS find bar. Around it:

Choose a component… and Insert selector: inserts a component’s CSS selector at the cursor,
for search or the table of contents for instance.
In the inspector under Available CSS variables: a click inserts var(--name), a click on the
colour its value; with ⌥ it is copied instead of inserted.
Callout colors: a click on a callout type inserts a scaffold for its colours.
Colors and fonts in effect: what applies right now, light and dark, with a font sample.

Checking before the build
An error in the SCSS makes the whole build fail. QuartzHub therefore checks with the project’s Sass:

On opening the tab and after saving, it checks all stylesheets together. At the top it then says
“SCSS compiles without errors.” or the error with a link to file and line. Check again checks
once more.
Check code in the toolbar checks only the open file, unsaved too.

If no Sass is installed in the project, QuartzHub says it cannot check instead of giving the
all-clear. A CSS error also appears on the overview (3.1).
Projects from older versions
Two notes appear only in projects set up with an early version:

Move now moves load order, fonts and variables out of custom.scss into the file
_quartzcontrol.scss of their own.
Merge combines the old templates’ stylesheets into the twelve files of the new split and keeps
every rule.

Both take a snapshot first and only work without unsaved changes.

en/5-design/09-templates.title: 5.9 – Templates
en/5-design/09-templates.content:
A template is a single file ending in .qtpl that carries a project’s design: colours, theme, CSS,
fonts, layout, frames, plugins, translations, content too if you like. After applying it, another
project is set up like the one it comes from. Templates creates and applies them. The page saves
nothing by itself; creating and applying are done with the buttons.

“Create a template” with the parts at the top, “Apply template” below.
The parts
A template consists of up to twelve parts; when creating as when applying you choose which:

























































PartWhat it carriesNotes (content/)the files in the content folder; usually not wanted for a design, but for a template that explains itselfColours & fontsthe base colours for light and dark, the three fonts and where they come fromCommunity themethe chosen theme with all its settings; the package is installed when applyingCSS variablesyour own values under VariablesCustom CSScustom.scss and all your own stylesheets with their load orderFont filesthe fonts you brought yourself and their rulesStatic fileseverything under quartz/static except the fonts: logos, pictures, snippetsLayoutwhich component appears where, per page type, and the breakpointsCustom framesthe frames you built; registered afresh in the target projectPluginsall plugin entries with options, order and positionTranslationsthe changed texts from Quartz’s language filesTheme presetsthe saved presets
Creating a template
Under Create a template: Template name (prefilled with the project name) and Description
(optional), then the parts with their figures, such as “58 plugins, 41 active”. What the project
has is ticked.
For Translations, Scope chooses between Only your changes and All texts. QuartzHub only
knows what was changed since you edited a text under Configuration ▸ Translations
(4.4); for languages before that, take “All texts”.
Save template… asks for the place and writes the file. Static files may be at most 25 MB together,
the notes at most 100 MB: a template is a design, not a backup. A part above that is not in the list;
a note below it says why.
What a template gives away
A template names the folder of the project it comes from and carries whatever the chosen parts
contain. Before passing one on, check what is in it, especially Notes (content/), Static files and
Plugins, whose options may contain addresses, for instance.

Applying a template
Under Apply template:

Basic template loads the template also offered when creating a project
(2.2) from GitHub. Only the design parts are ticked, not
content, layout, plugins, translations and presets.
Choose a template… opens a .qtpl file. Everything it contains is ticked. Templates in the
old format, a folder instead of a file, carry the mark Old format and can be applied too.

Below are name, description, date and origin of the template and, after a check, what each part would
do in this project: how much is new, replaced, kept as is or refused. The check writes nothing.
On conflict:

Template wins: what the project already has is replaced by the template.
Project wins: what the project already has stays; only what is missing is added. Colours & fonts
and the layout are then not taken over at all, not even in part.

If something has to be installed, a theme or a plugin, it says so below; that needs a network
connection.
Apply template asks once, takes a snapshot (“Before template import”) and applies the parts one
after another. If one fails, the others carry on. At the end it says “Done: everything applied,
nothing left open.” or lists what did not work or stayed unchanged.
A few things a template never does:

It does not write into a linked vault; if the content folder is a link, Notes (content/) is skipped.
It does not replace a project image you chose yourself (4.3).
It writes nothing outside the project folder.
With quartz-forms, the project keeps its sending, keys, spam protection and forms; only missing
forms are added.

If you do not like the result, the snapshot leads back (7.3).

en/5-design/index.title: 5 – Design
en/5-design/index.content:
The Design group has three pages. Layout sets what stands where on the page. Styles sets
how it looks: colours, fonts, CSS. Templates packs a finished design into a file you take over
into another project.

The layers: in which order basics, theme, variables and custom CSS
override each other. Once you have read it, you stop searching why a colour has no effect.

Layout

Layout overview: which component appears on which page type.
Components: the stage on which components are moved.
Frames: building page grids of your own.

Styles

Basics: base colours, fonts and how they are delivered.
Community themes: ready-made colour schemes.
Variables: changing single CSS variables precisely.
Custom CSS: writing stylesheets yourself.

Templates

Templates: saving a design as a file and applying it.

en/6-publishing/01-the-preview.title: 6.1 – The preview
en/6-publishing/01-the-preview.content:
The preview is Quartz’s own dev server: Quartz builds the site, serves it on the Mac and rebuilds on
every change. Preview & Build shows it in the middle of the window.

The running preview. Width and scale at the top, the output below, the server on the right.
Starting and stopping
Start in the toolbar, or Project ▸ Start Server (⌘R) from any window of the project. Then the
button reads Stop (⌘.), with Restart next to it. The state is in the inspector: Stopped,
Starting…, Running, Stopping… or Error.
The server counts as started when it answers. The first time that takes as long as a build, half a
minute or more for a large site. After that, Quartz rebuilds after every change, to the notes as to the
configuration, and the page reloads by itself.
Before every start QuartzHub puts the project in order: it rewrites your own frames, puts back a
missing line in custom.scss and fetches missing fonts. What it does is in the output.
The start is refused, with the reason in red at the top, when

the project’s npm packages are missing, after a fresh clone for instance; Install on the overview
fetches them;
a server QuartzHub did not start is already running for the same project
(6.4).

The preview in the window

Desktop, Tablet, Mobile: the site is built at a fitting width, desktop at least 1280
pixels, and fitted into the window. Next to it are width and scale, such as “1280 px · 73%”.
Fit or 100%: scale down, or show at real size and scroll sideways.
Reload preview and Open in browser.

Links within the site open in the preview, links to the outside in the browser.
Server settings
In the inspector under Server settings:

Port (default 8080) and WS port (3001, for the automatic reload). If a port is in use, the
server takes the next free one at start and says so in the output.
Remote dev host (optional): only for a preview behind a tunnel, from another computer for
instance. The server then does not move to other ports.

The settings apply until QuartzHub quits. They can only be changed with the server stopped.
What happens to running servers when QuartzHub quits is set in the settings
(2.5).

en/6-publishing/02-the-build.title: 6.2 – The build
en/6-publishing/02-the-build.content:
A build produces the finished site once: HTML, CSS, pictures, everything that goes onto a server. The
preview builds too, but only for itself; publishing needs a build.
Building

Build now (hammer) in the toolbar of Preview & Build,
Project ▸ Run build (⌘B) from any window of the project,
Run build on the overview,
Build now under Publish.

During the build, the inspector says since when it has been running and what Quartz is doing:
preparing, reading the notes, writing the pages. Then “Successful in 12.3s” or “Failed in …”, and
what Quartz said about it is in the output (6.3).
One-off build shows when the site was last built, with the number and size of the files, and
Open folder. QuartzHub reads this from the output folder itself.
The output folder
The default is public/ in the project. Output folder (optional) sets another one, in the project
or elsewhere. It also applies to Publish: uploads come from the same folder.
Every build empties its output folder
Quartz deletes everything in the output folder before each build. QuartzHub therefore refuses folders
that cannot take that: the project folder itself, a folder containing the project, the home folder,
and folders of the project such as content/ or quartz/. If a folder holds files that do not look
like a build, QuartzHub asks first.

The preview always builds into public/, whatever this setting says. While it runs, a build cannot
write into public/ at the same time; QuartzHub says so and does not build.
Every way to build uses the same saved output folder. When the field holds a new folder not yet
confirmed with Return, Build now takes it first; a folder QuartzHub refuses is not built into.
When a build is needed
Before every publish that transfers files. Publish does not build by itself; it uploads what is in
the output folder and says when there is nothing there yet
(6.12).

en/6-publishing/03-reading-the-output.title: 6.3 – Reading the output
en/6-publishing/03-reading-the-output.content:
At the bottom of Preview & Build is the Output, in two consoles side by side: on the left the
preview server’s, on the right the last build’s. The grip above can be dragged; the output can also be
folded, and the preview then gets the room.

Preview stopped, a build’s output at the bottom right.
Colours

Normal text: what Quartz itself prints.
Orange: a sentence from QuartzHub about a run that continues, such as “Port 8080 is in use, the
server takes 8081 instead.” or what it put in order before the start.
Red: Quartz’s error output, or an error from QuartzHub, such as a refused build.

Clear output empties a console. Text can be selected and copied with ⌘C, for an error message for
instance. Each console keeps roughly the last thousand lines while QuartzHub runs, even when you leave
the page; after a restart they are empty.
What Quartz says
Quartz’s output comes unchanged. A few lines come up often:





































LineMeaningParsing input filesQuartz is reading the notes.Emitting filesQuartz is writing the pages.Done processing … files in …The build is finished.Started a Quartz server listening at http://localhost:8080The preview is running.Detected change, rebuilding…A file changed; the preview rebuilds.[200] /pathThe preview served a page.[404] /pathSomething was requested that does not exist, a picture with a wrong path for instance.
Warnings in square brackets name the plugin they come from, such as [links] for links to pages that
do not exist. They do not stop the build.
When the build fails
A build mostly fails at one of three places:

At the CSS. An error in a stylesheet. Styles ▸ Custom CSS shows it with file and line, as
does the overview (5.8).
At a note. Broken frontmatter (a colon without quotes, say) or an embed that does not exist.
Quartz names the file; fix it in the editor.
At a plugin. A plugin that is missing or does not fit this Quartz. Quartz names it; Plugins ▸
Installed shows what Quartz’s own check says about it (4.5).

The most important line is usually at the end of the red output. The overview also reports a crashed
server under Needs attention.

en/6-publishing/04-other-servers.title: 6.4 – Other servers
en/6-publishing/04-other-servers.content:
A Quartz server runs as a process of its own and can outlive QuartzHub: when you choose “Keep running”
at quit, when QuartzHub crashes or when someone starts Quartz in the Terminal. QuartzHub finds such
servers.
Servers running on this machine
This section in the inspector of Preview & Build lists every Quartz server on the Mac, whoever
started it. Refresh searches again; otherwise QuartzHub searches when the window comes back to the
front and when one of its own servers starts or ends.
Each row shows:

the address; a click opens it in the browser;
Started by QuartzHub (in this session) or Started elsewhere (everything else);
the project, if QuartzHub knows it, otherwise the site’s title or the folder;
process number, WebSocket port and since when it has been running;
Stop server.

A server QuartzHub did not start is never stopped by it on its own. Stop server asks first,
because whoever started it may be working with it right now.
Why this matters
Two servers for the same project would build into the same folder. QuartzHub therefore starts no
second one and says which is already running. If a port is taken, but not by a recognisable Quartz
server, the section says so; the preview then takes another port.
At start and at quit
At start QuartzHub asks about servers it started itself in an earlier session that are still
running: Keep running or stop them.
At quit it asks about this session’s servers, depending on the setting
(2.5). Before that it asks about unsaved changes and about running
work such as an update or a publish.

en/6-publishing/05-git-sync.title: 6.5 – Git Sync
en/6-publishing/05-git-sync.content:
A Quartz project is a git repository. Git Sync uploads it to a repository on the net and fetches
changes from there: as a backup, to carry on working on a second Mac, or as the basis for GitHub Pages
(6.8). If you only want to publish, you do not need Git Sync.

A project without a repository on the net, the section for creating one below.
Repository state

Branch: the branch checked out. Quartz projects stand on v5.
Upstream and Sync state: whether the branch has a counterpart on the net and how many commits
are still to be pushed or fetched; “Up to date with the remote” when nothing is missing. This is as
of the last exchange; the page does not ask the net itself.
Working tree: local changes and conflicts.
origin: the address of the repository on the net, with Open on GitHub for GitHub.
Last commit.

At the bottom, Local changes lists the changed files: new, modified, deleted, renamed, untracked,
conflict. Refresh in the toolbar reads the state again.
Creating a repository on GitHub
A new project deliberately has no repository on the net, so nothing ends up at Quartz itself by
accident. Create a repository on GitHub creates one under your account and enters it as origin:

Repository name, prefilled with the project’s name;
Private: on a free account, GitHub Pages is only available for public repositories.

This needs a personal access token with the “repo” scope under Settings ▸ Connections
(6.7). A repository elsewhere, on Codeberg say, is
entered as origin in the Terminal (git remote add origin <address>).
Push and pull

Commit changes first (on by default): puts all local changes into one commit, with the Commit
message or “Quartz sync: ”.
Pull fetches the branch v5 from origin and merges it.
Push uploads the current branch, as a force push: what exists only on the net is lost.
Push + pull does both.

QuartzHub uses Quartz’s own quartz sync for this. Below, it then says “Successful.” or “Failed.”
with the output.
Signing in: for a repository on github.com over https, QuartzHub uses the token from the settings.
For ssh addresses and other providers, git’s own keys and credential helpers apply, as in the
Terminal.
Force push means: this Mac wins
If two computers work on the same project: first Pull, then change, then Push. Whoever pushes
first overwrites what the other computer uploaded.

When a pull fails
If both sides changed the same file, a conflict remains: the working tree shows it, and at the top it
says “A merge has been started and is not finished.” Abort merge goes back to the state before the
pull; what was staged by hand since would be lost with it, and QuartzHub asks first then. QuartzHub cannot resolve a conflict; that is done in an editor or in the Terminal.
What does not come along

node_modules/ and public/: they are made afresh on the other computer
(2.3).
.quartz-gui/, meaning your frames, snapshots and targets: the folder is in .gitignore. Your own
frames are therefore copied by hand or taken from a snapshot
(3.1).
A linked vault: Quartz uploads the notes as files; on the other computer the content folder has to be
linked again (4.2).

Books (quartz-books/) come along.

en/6-publishing/06-documents.title: 6.6 – Documents
en/6-publishing/06-documents.content:
A book is a selection of the site’s pages in an order, with a cover and a table of contents.
Documents creates books; they are put out through a target of the type “Document” under
Publish, as PDF, ePub or a single HTML file. The PDF of this handbook was made that way.

A book following the site’s navigation. Its settings on the right.
Creating books
➕ New book asks for the title and creates a book that follows the site’s navigation at first. Each
book is a file under quartz-books/ in the project and comes along with Git Sync. The file is named
after that title, “Garden notes” becomes garden-notes.json, and keeps the name when you change the
title later; the exported files are named the same. The name is shown under the title while you create
the book.
Save (⌘S) writes changes; Discard takes them back.
The pages
QuartzHub reads the list of pages from the last build. Without a build it says so and points to
Preview & Build. The content index has to be on as well (4.1).

Following the navigation (default): the book takes the order of the site’s navigation. Untick a
page to leave it out. Pages the navigation does not show are listed below.
Own order: copies the navigation into a list of its own. Drag pages into place or move them with
Arrange ▸ Move Up/Move Down (⌥⌘↑, ⌥⌘↓). + Heading inserts a heading such as “Appendix”;
Take in adds a page that is not in the navigation. Follow the navigation again drops the own
list.

The start page of the chosen folder always comes first.
Settings in the inspector

Title (empty: the site’s title), Subtitle, Author.
Language, if the site has several (4.8).
Folder: only the pages in this folder; empty for the whole site.
Picture on the cover: a path in the project; empty for the project image.
Table of contents (in the PDF with page numbers), Links to this page at the end of each page,
Register of tags at the end.
Links to pages outside the book: To the website (needs a base URL) or As text.
Paper size (PDF): A4, A5 or Letter, plus Landscape.

Putting it out
Under Publish, create a target of the type Document: Target folder, Book and the
Formats PDF, ePub, HTML (one file) (6.7). Export
now writes the files, <book>.pdf and so on; a running export can be cancelled.
A PDF has a cover, the table of contents with page numbers, bookmarks by heading and a footer with
title and page number. Formulas and diagrams are drawn as pictures; forms, videos and embedded pages
are replaced by a sentence with their address.
If QuartzHub finds faults, such as pictures that do not load or links without a target, it writes
nothing and says what it found. For formulas and diagrams the export loads stylesheets and scripts
from the net; without a connection they are missing.
Upload documents too on another target uploads the last exported files with the site into the
folder downloads/; QuartzHub shows a link for it you can put on a page.

en/6-publishing/07-connections-and-targe.title: 6.7 – Connections and targets
en/6-publishing/07-connections-and-targe.content:
Publishing takes two things:

A connection is an account at a provider: a server login, a build hook, a token for GitHub.
Connections apply to all projects and live under Settings ▸ Connections.
A target belongs to one project and says where its site goes: which connection, which folder on
the server, which branch, whether to delete. Targets live under Publish.

That way two projects use the same web space with one connection and two targets in different folders.

Two targets, a folder and a document. Below, the “Changes” section, with no diff computed yet.
Which target fits?








































I have …TargetChaptera GitHub account and want to pay nothingGit branch with GitHub Pages6.8a web space at a hosting providerSFTP (or rsync), FTP if nothing else6.9a server of my own or a NASSFTP with rsync6.9Netlify, Cloudflare Pages or Vercel, which build themselvesWebhook6.11a folder something else passes on (cloud folder, share)Folder6.10a book as PDF or ePubDocument6.6
Codeberg Pages and GitLab Pages also go through Git branch.
Creating connections
Settings ▸ Connections (⌘, or Manage connections under Publish):

GitHub: a Personal access token. Save & check asks GitHub whether it is valid and shows
Valid with the account name, Rejected or Cannot check. For the marketplace a token without
permissions is enough; repositories and GitHub Pages need the “repo” scope.
SFTP / SSH: Host, Port (22), Username and the Authentication: Password,
Private key (as a file, usually from ~/.ssh, or pasted) or SSH agent. Your own
~/.ssh/config keeps applying.
FTP: host, port (21), username, password and FTPS (encrypted), on by default. Without FTPS,
password and files cross the network unencrypted.
Webhook: the provider’s Webhook URL, https only.

Passwords, keys, tokens and webhook URLs live in the macOS keychain, never in the project. A connection
shows how many targets use it; deleting it warns.
Host key: at the first SFTP connection, QuartzHub shows the server’s fingerprint and asks whether it
is right. The provider names the fingerprint. Connect and remember stores it for all projects. If
it changes later, QuartzHub refuses the connection; only Forget host key makes it ask again, and
only do that when the server was demonstrably set up anew.
Creating targets
➕ New target under Publish: Name, Type and, depending on the type, the fields the
following chapters describe. For SFTP, FTP and Webhook you choose the Connection; New …
connection creates one without leaving the dialog.
For all types except Git branch and Document there is:

Also delete removed files at the target (on by default): what disappeared from the site
disappears at the target too.
Never publish (one path per line): paths from the build that are never uploaded, such as
.htaccess when the server has its own.
Upload documents too (6.6).

Targets live in .quartz-gui/publish-targets.json, without passwords. A copy of the project does not
get them (2.4).
The base URL first
If the base URL still says localhost, Publish says so at the top. Otherwise links, RSS feed and
preview images of a published site point nowhere (4.1).

en/6-publishing/08-github-pages.title: 6.8 – GitHub Pages
en/6-publishing/08-github-pages.content:
GitHub Pages serves a site from a branch of a repository, free and over https. QuartzHub puts the
build as one commit onto a branch of its own, usually gh-pages, and points Pages at that branch.
GitHub Actions are not needed.
Setting it up once

Token: under Settings ▸ Connections, enter a personal access token with the “repo” scope
(6.7).
Repository: under Git Sync ▸ Create a repository on GitHub. On a free account it has to be
public (6.5).
Base URL: under Configuration ▸ Site, enter the future address, usually
name.github.io/repository, or your own domain.
Target: under Publish, a new target of the type Git branch, Provider GitHub Pages,
Branch gh-pages. The branch must not be the one the project itself stands on.
Switching Pages on: in the GitHub Pages section below the target, Point at “gh-pages”.

Then build and Publish now (6.12). A few minutes later
the site is at the address the section names.
The GitHub Pages section
It shows whether Pages is Published, Building, Failed or Never built, the site’s address
and which branch it comes from. Reload status asks GitHub again.
Custom domain: such as wiki.example.org. At the domain’s provider, a DNS entry has to point at
GitHub; GitHub describes how. Save settings writes the domain; GitHub puts it as a file CNAME into
the branch, and QuartzHub keeps it at every publish. Enforce HTTPS only works once GitHub has issued
the certificate, a few minutes after setting the domain.
What happens on publishing
The branch is replaced entirely by the current build every time (force push), in a single commit
without history. That is why QuartzHub asks first. If nothing changed, nothing is uploaded. The
project’s hooks do not run.
Codeberg Pages serves the branch pages the same way. GitLab additionally needs a CI job that serves
the files; the branch alone publishes nothing there.

en/6-publishing/09-to-a-web-space.title: 6.9 – To a web space
en/6-publishing/09-to-a-web-space.content:
For a web space at a hosting provider or a server of your own there are three ways. A connection under
Settings ▸ Connections comes first (6.7).





















WayWhenSFTPthe normal case; every host with SSH access can do itSFTP with rsyncfaster, compares against the server; needs a key and rsync on the serverFTPonly when the host offers nothing else, and then with FTPS
The target
A new target of the type SFTP or FTP, with the matching Connection, and:

Remote path: the folder on the server the site goes into, such as httpdocs or
/var/www/example.org. Without a leading slash it counts from the login directory; on a web space
that is the normal case. Which folder serves the site, the host tells you.
Transfer (SFTP only): SFTP (file by file) or rsync (faster, compares against the server).
Also delete removed files at the target, Never publish.

QuartzHub creates the site’s folder, but not folders above it.
Deleting and the login directory
With deleting on, QuartzHub refuses the login directory itself (/, ., ~) as the path: it would
be emptied. The site belongs in a subfolder.

SFTP or rsync
SFTP compares the build with a list of what QuartzHub last sent to this target and transfers only
what is new or changed. It does not notice what someone changes or deletes directly on the server; for
that there is Upload everything again (6.12).
rsync asks the server itself what is there; the comparison is right even after changes by hand.
rsync needs:

a connection with Private key as a file or SSH agent, no password;
a confirmed host key: publish once via SFTP, then rsync can be chosen;
rsync on the server.

The dialog says what is missing.
rsync deletes everything that is not part of the build
With deleting on, rsync removes every file in the target folder the build does not have, including
files QuartzHub never uploaded, such as an .htaccess or a folder of downloads. What should stay goes
under Never publish, or the site gets a folder of its own.

FTP
FTP transfers file by file like SFTP, after the list of the last run. Without FTPS the password and
the files cross the network in plain text; QuartzHub then warns.
When it does not work
QuartzHub says why, with the server’s name: not reachable, port refused, login refused (with its own
sentence for password, key and agent), no answer for 60 seconds. If the server is in your own network,
a NAS for instance, QuartzHub needs permission for the local network
(1.2).

en/6-publishing/10-to-a-folder.title: 6.10 – To a folder
en/6-publishing/10-to-a-folder.content:
A target of the type Folder copies the site into a folder: on the Mac, on a drive or a share.
Useful when something else passes the files on (a cloud folder, a NAS that serves them itself), or to
see what would be uploaded.

Target folder: a full path, via Select. It must not lie inside the build folder or contain it,
and must not be the project folder. The first time, QuartzHub creates it, along with missing folders
above it.
Also delete removed files at the target and Never publish as with the other targets.

As with SFTP, only what is new or changed is transferred. Each file is first written under a temporary
name and then renamed, so a sync program never sees half a file.
If the target was used before and the folder is now gone or empty, QuartzHub stops: usually a drive is
not connected. If the folder really should be created afresh, choose Upload everything again first
(6.12).

en/6-publishing/11-webhook.title: 6.11 – Webhook
en/6-publishing/11-webhook.content:
Some providers build the site themselves, from the repository: Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel or a
CI of your own. A webhook triggers that build. No files are transferred; the provider takes the
state from the repository.
That also means: what is not in the repository does not arrive. So a Push under Git Sync comes
before the webhook (6.5).
Setting it up

At the provider, create a build hook; it gives an address for it, such as
api.netlify.com/build_hooks/….
Under Settings ▸ Connections, create a Webhook connection with this address. The address is a
secret: whoever knows it can trigger builds. QuartzHub keeps it in the keychain and only shows its
beginning.
Under Publish, a target of the type Webhook with this connection.

Publish now asks briefly and then sends a request to the address. If the provider answers with
success, the build has been triggered there; whether it succeeds, the provider shows.

en/6-publishing/12-what-gets-uploaded.title: 6.12 – What gets uploaded
en/6-publishing/12-what-gets-uploaded.content:
Before QuartzHub transfers anything, it shows what changed since the last run to this target. Under
Publish this is in the Changes section below the selected target.
The changes

Build now builds the site and then computes the changes again.
Refresh diff computes them again without building. QuartzHub does not compute them by itself.
Output folder: the same as under Preview & Build (6.2).

Below it says “Added: 3 · Changed: 12 · Removed: 1” and a list for each. For SFTP, FTP, folder and rsync,
each file has a tick: without it the file is left out of this run, and next time it is listed again.
Leaving it out for good is done with Never publish in the target.
How the comparison works:





























TargetCompared withSFTP, FTP, folderthe list of what QuartzHub last sent to this target, offlineSFTP with rsyncwhat is on the serverGit branchthe branch on the netDocumentwhether the files are there alreadyWebhooknothing; nothing is transferred
Upload everything again forgets the list of the last run; the preview then offers the whole build
again. That is needed when something was deleted on the server by hand or a transfer broke off. A
target that is pointed at another folder or connection also uploads everything next time. With rsync
the button is not there: rsync compares with the server anyway.
The run
Publish now in the toolbar asks first, with the number of files to upload and delete; for a Git
branch with the note that the branch is replaced. It does not build by itself; what is in the output
folder is uploaded. No snapshot is taken.
During the run, a bar shows which file is being handled. You can leave the page; the run carries on,
and at quit QuartzHub asks. Only an export can be cancelled.
Afterwards it says Published successfully., Publish failed. or, if the server refused single
deletions, how many files stayed; QuartzHub tries them again next time. The output below lists every
file: ↑ uploaded, ✗ deleted.
The usual order
Save, Build now, look at the list, Publish now. If the list holds more than expected, take a
look before pressing.

en/6-publishing/index.title: 6 – Publishing
en/6-publishing/index.content:
The Publishing group has four pages: Preview & Build shows the site and builds it, Git
sync keeps the project in step with a repository, Documents makes books from it, and
Publish takes the result where it should go.
Preview & Build

The preview: the site in the window while you write.
The build: the finished files, and where they go.
Reading the output: what Quartz says, and what of it matters.
Other servers: previews QuartzHub did not start itself.

Git Sync and documents

Git Sync: keeping and sharing the project in a repository.
Documents: books as PDF, ePub or HTML.

Publish

Connections and targets: the difference, and which target fits.
GitHub Pages
To a web space: SFTP, rsync, FTP.
To a folder
Webhook: Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel.
What gets uploaded: the preview of the changes and the run.

en/7-maintenance/01-updates.title: 7.1 – Updates
en/7-maintenance/01-updates.content:
Quartz keeps evolving, and so do the plugins. Updates says whether there is something new and brings
it into the project. QuartzHub takes a snapshot before every update.

Quartz is up to date, and so are the plugins from the marketplace.
Checking
When the page opens, QuartzHub asks GitHub whether there is a newer version of Quartz and whether the
installed plugins have newer ones. Check again in the toolbar asks once more. Without a network it
says Cannot check, not “Up to date”.
Quartz’s core
The line shows which version is installed and which is the latest, and how many changes are missing.
Next to it Up to date, Update available, Unfinished or Cannot check. New in Quartz …
unfolds the changes Quartz itself wrote down for them.
If the project’s remote quartz-upstream does not point to jackyzha0/quartz, to a copy of your own for
instance, a note below says that Run update fetches from there while the line shows the state of
jackyzha0/quartz.
Run update asks first and then:

takes a snapshot (“Before core update”);
fetches the new version of Quartz and merges it with the project. Your own packages in
package.json are set aside briefly for this and put back afterwards;
reinstalls the npm packages;
builds the site once.

Afterwards it says “The core update is complete.”, with the output to unfold and Open the snapshot
from before the update. From Quartz 5.1 on, QuartzHub then runs Quartz’s own check of the plugins
and says whether entries should be moved (4.5).
Commit first, then update
An update merges Quartz’s changes with the project. Uncommitted changes to Quartz’s files can get in
the way; QuartzHub then names them. If you use Git Sync, commit first
(6.5).

When it gets stuck

Conflicts: if Quartz and the project changed the same place, the merge stops. The page names the
files. Abort merge goes back to the state before the update; otherwise resolve the conflicts in an
editor and run the update again. Your own texts in the language files are guarded by the update
protection (4.4).
Unfinished: if npm install failed or your own packages are still missing, the page says so.
Run update catches up.
Back: the snapshot from before the update leads to the old state. For the Updates page to report
the old state too, switch on Also reset the project commit when restoring
(7.3).

Plugins
These are the plugins added through the marketplace or the command line. Quartz’s built-in plugins come
with the core update. Each row shows the installed and the latest version and Up to date,
Update or Cannot check; Local means the plugin lives in the project itself (one of your
frames, for instance) and has no source on the net.
Update and Update all ask first, take a snapshot and have Quartz fetch the latest version. The
configuration stays as it is.
For a bug report
From Quartz 5.1 on, the inspector has Show Quartz info: Quartz sums up its version, the environment
and the plugins as text you can copy into a bug report for Quartz or a plugin.

en/7-maintenance/02-snapshots.title: 7.2 – Snapshots
en/7-maintenance/02-snapshots.content:
A snapshot is a copy of the whole project at one point in time. It stays in the project, is never
uploaded and does not touch your git history. It is there for getting things back when something went
wrong; sharing with other computers is what Git Sync is for.

A snapshot marked “Yours”. On the right, whether the content folder is included.
What is in it
Everything in the project except what a build or an install produces anew: node_modules/, public/,
the downloaded plugins and caches. So configuration, stylesheets, your frames, translations, books,
targets, and the notes if the content folder is a real folder.
Include the content folder (inspector, on by default) takes the notes along or leaves them out. A
linked vault is never included; back that up with Obsidian or Time Machine.
The snapshots live in .quartz-gui/snapshots.git/, a git repository of their own.
When QuartzHub takes one
By itself, before every larger change. The Reason column says before what:









































ReasonBeforeBefore config changesaving the configuration, under Configuration, Layout, Styles, Plugins; at most one every 15 minutesBefore plugin changeinstalling, removing, updating or moving a plugin; registering a new frameBefore core updatethe update of QuartzBefore content switchswitching the content folderBefore template importapplying a templateBefore the styles movedmoving old stylesheetsBefore restoreevery restoreOld config backupconfiguration backups from early versions
If nothing changed since the last snapshot, QuartzHub takes no new one; before a core update it takes
one anyway.
Taking one yourself: ➕ Take snapshot in the toolbar, with a name such as “before switching
themes”, or Take snapshot on the overview, without a name. These carry the reason Yours.
How long they stay
Your own snapshots and those before a core update stay until you delete them. The other automatic ones
are thinned out over time:

younger than a day: all;
up to a week: one per day;
up to eight weeks: one per week;
older: one per month.

The newest one of each stays. To keep a state for sure, take a snapshot yourself.
The list
Time, Name, Reason and, in a wide window, Project commit: the project’s commit when
the snapshot was taken (a dash without a git repository). The context menu has Export as ZIP and Delete. What a snapshot changes compared
with today and how to get it back is in 7.3.

en/7-maintenance/03-restoring.title: 7.3 – Restoring
en/7-maintenance/03-restoring.content:
Comparing
A click on a snapshot under Snapshots compares it with the current state. The inspector shows
Compared with the current state: how many files differ, and each with its state:

new since: did not exist then; restoring deletes it;
deleted since: existed then; restoring brings it back;
changed: the symbol next to it shows the difference line by line.

If Include the content folder is off or the content folder is a link, the notes are left out of
comparing and restoring.
Restoring

Restore everything puts the whole project back to the snapshot. Files that did not exist then are
deleted.
Restore selection puts back only the ticked files.

Both ask first and take a snapshot of the current state beforehand (“Before restore”); a restore can
itself be taken back. If package.json changed, QuartzHub then reinstalls the npm packages. While it
runs, QuartzHub asks at quit.
Also reset the project commit appears when the snapshot was taken on a different git commit than
today, before a core update for instance. It also resets the project’s git history; only then does
Updates report the old state of Quartz again.
The notes follow the Include the content folder switch: with it off they stay as they are, and git
then shows them as changes against the old commit. With it on they come back from the snapshot; their
state before is kept in the “Before restore” snapshot.
A pushed commit
If the commit was already pushed, the local state differs from the repository on the net after the
reset.

Exporting as ZIP
Export as ZIP in the context menu or the inspector writes a snapshot’s state into a ZIP file, to get
a single file out without resetting anything, for instance.
Set-aside content folders
Switching the content folder sets the old one aside (4.2). These
folders are listed under Snapshots in a list of their own, with time and size or the target of the
link back then. Restore puts one back and sets the current one aside as well.

en/7-maintenance/04-cleaning-up.title: 7.4 – Cleaning up
en/7-maintenance/04-cleaning-up.content:
QuartzHub clears most things itself: it thins out old automatic snapshots, deletes the logs of earlier
previews at the next start of the preview, and removes leftover work folders of export, relay and SSH at
app start. For the rest there are these places:

node_modules/ and public/ can be deleted at any time: the overview then offers Install, and the
next build creates public/ anew.

en/7-maintenance/index.title: 7 – Maintenance
en/7-maintenance/index.content:
A site that runs needs little care. Now and then there is something new from Quartz or a plugin, and
sometimes something goes wrong. That is what the Maintenance group is for.

Updates: bringing Quartz and the plugins up to date.
Snapshots: what they are, when they are taken, what they contain.
Restoring: bringing back a snapshot or single files.
Cleaning up: what piles up and how to get rid of it.

en/8-reference/04-known-limits.title: 8.4 – Known limits
en/8-reference/04-known-limits.content:
Computer and distribution

macOS 26 or later, Apple silicon only. There is no version for Intel Macs, Linux or Windows.
Not notarised by Apple. The first start needs “Open Anyway” once
(1.2).
Updating is by hand. When there is a newer version, the Projects window says so
(2.1); downloading and replacing it is up to you
(1.2).
A new project needs the network: Quartz comes from GitHub, and so does the basic template.

Deliberately so

No zooming of the interface; text size follows macOS.
The desktop preview is built at 1280 pixels and fitted in.
The export window for PDFs is always light, so diagrams are too.

Not there yet

PDFs are not tagged for screen readers.

What to watch out for

Push in Git Sync is a force push (6.5).
rsync with deleting on removes everything in the target folder that is not part of the build
(6.9).
Set-aside content folders are the only copy; snapshots do not contain them
(4.2).
Older automatic snapshots are thinned out (7.2).

en/8-reference/05-glossary.title: 8.5 – Glossary
en/8-reference/05-glossary.content:
Base URL
The address the finished site is reachable at, without https://, such as name.github.io/project.
Quartz builds links, the RSS feed and preview images from it (4.1).
Branch
A line of development in a git repository. Quartz projects stand on the branch v5; GitHub Pages
usually serves the site from a branch of its own, gh-pages
(6.8).
Breakpoint
The window width from which a site switches to the tablet or mobile layout. For your own frames 1200
and 800 pixels, adjustable (5.4).
Build
Producing the finished site from the notes: HTML, CSS, pictures, all in the output folder, usually
public/ (6.2).
Callout
A highlighted box in a note, written in Obsidian as > [!note]. Quartz shows it on the site the same
way.
Commit
A saved state in a git repository. Git Sync puts local changes into one commit
(6.5).
Community theme
A ready-made colour scheme from the @quartz-themes catalogue that lies on top of the base colours
(5.6).
Component
A visible part of a page, such as search, table of contents or graph, with a position such as header
or sidebar (5.3).
Connection and target
A connection is an account at a provider and applies to all projects; a target belongs to one
project and says where its site goes (6.7).
Content folder
The folder content/ in the project with the notes the site is made from: a real folder or a link to
a vault (4.2).
CSS variable
A named value in CSS, such as --secondary for the colour of links. Almost all colours and fonts of a
Quartz site are variables (5.7).
Dev server
Quartz’s own server for the preview. It builds the site, serves it on the Mac and rebuilds on every
change (6.1).
Frame
The grid of a page: which areas there are and how they lie. Quartz brings three; your own are built
under Layout ▸ Frames (5.4).
Frontmatter
The block between --- at the start of a note, with entries such as title, tags or draft.
Marketplace
The catalogue of the quartz-community’s plugins on GitHub, under Plugins ▸ Marketplace
(4.10).
npm
Node’s package manager. Quartz and many plugins are npm packages; they live in the project in
node_modules/. QuartzHub brings npm along.
Page type
A kind of page Quartz builds: content pages, folder pages, tag pages, the 404 page and more depending
on the plugins (5.2).
Plugin
An extension of Quartz. Almost everything Quartz does, a plugin does: reading Markdown, resolving
links, search, the sidebar (4.5).
Preset
A saved combination of a community theme with its settings
(5.6).
Project
A folder holding a Quartz site: configuration, stylesheets, plugins and content folder
(2).
Quartz
A program that builds a website from Markdown notes, a “static site generator”. It understands
Obsidian’s wikilinks, callouts and embedded pictures. QuartzHub works with Quartz 5
(quartz.jzhao.xyz).
Repository
A folder under version control with git, with its whole history. Every Quartz project is one; on the
net it lives at GitHub, for instance (6.5).
Snapshot
A saved state of the whole project, which QuartzHub takes by itself before larger changes and which
you can go back to (7.2).
Token
A key with which a program identifies itself to a service, here the personal access token for GitHub.
It lives in the keychain (6.7).
Vault
A folder of notes managed by Obsidian. A project’s content folder can point to a vault or a folder in
it (4.2).
Wikilink
A link in double square brackets, such as [[Note]], as Obsidian writes it. Quartz understands it and
turns it into a link on the site.

en/index.title: QuartzHub
en/index.content:
QuartzHub is a Mac app for Quartz, a static site generator. Without it,
you run Quartz from the command line and edit its configuration in a text editor; with it, you click.
This handbook explains every window and every page of QuartzHub: what it does, when you need it and
what is better left alone there.

A project’s overview: preview, build, publishing, snapshots and updates at a glance.
What QuartzHub can do
Notes become a website
An Obsidian vault or any folder becomes the content folder, linked if you want to keep writing in
Obsidian, copied if not. Switching later is possible without losing a note. →
4.2

Designing without writing CSS
Colours and fonts, community themes, the site’s CSS variables separately for light and dark,
stylesheets of your own. The page grid is made in an editor with the mouse, per screen width.
→ 5.1, 5.4

Plugins from a marketplace
Browse, install, set up, with a form instead of YAML. Navigations, additional content boxes,
languages and forms have editors of their own with a preview next to them.
→ 4.5

Looking before anyone else does
The preview runs in the window and rebuilds on every change, at the width of a desktop, tablet or
phone; Quartz’s output is below it. → 6.1

Books from the site
A selection of pages, in the order you want, as PDF or ePub, with a table of contents and formulas.
This handbook exists that way too. → 6.6

Publishing and coming back
GitHub Pages, a web space over SFTP, rsync or FTP, a folder, a webhook, with a preview of what will be
transferred. And before larger changes a snapshot to go back to. →
6.7, 7.2

Where to start

New here: 1.1 – What QuartzHub is, then
1.4 – Your first site.
Looking something up: Menus and shortcuts,
Glossary.

How to write notes so they make good pages is in the
Example handbook.

index.title: QuartzHub
index.content:
QuartzHub ist eine Mac-App für Quartz, einen Generator für statische
Websites. Ohne sie bedient man Quartz über die Kommandozeile und bearbeitet seine Konfiguration im
Texteditor; mit ihr klickt man. Dieses Handbuch erklärt jedes Fenster und jede Seite von QuartzHub:
was sie tut, wann man sie braucht und was man dort besser nicht tut.

Die Übersicht eines Projekts: Vorschau, Build, Veröffentlichen, Snapshots und Updates auf einen
Blick.
Was QuartzHub kann
Aus Notizen wird eine Website
Ein Obsidian-Vault oder irgendein Ordner wird zum Content-Ordner, verknüpft, wenn man in
Obsidian weiterschreiben will, kopiert, wenn nicht. Umstellen geht später, ohne eine Notiz zu
verlieren. → 4.2

Gestalten, ohne CSS zu schreiben
Farben und Schriften, Community-Themes, die CSS-Variablen der Website für hell und dunkel getrennt,
eigene Stylesheets. Das Seitenraster entsteht in einem Editor mit der Maus, je Bildschirmbreite.
→ 5.1, 5.4

Plugins aus einem Marktplatz
Durchsuchen, installieren, einstellen, mit einem Formular statt YAML. Navigationen, zusätzliche
Inhaltsboxen, Mehrsprachigkeit und Formulare haben eigene Editoren mit einer Vorschau daneben.
→ 4.5

Ansehen, bevor es jemand anders sieht
Die Vorschau läuft im Fenster und baut bei jeder Änderung neu, in der Breite eines Desktops,
Tablets oder Telefons; die Ausgabe von Quartz steht darunter. →
6.1

Bücher aus der Website
Eine Auswahl von Seiten, in der gewünschten Reihenfolge, als PDF oder ePub, mit Inhaltsverzeichnis
und Formeln. Auch dieses Handbuch gibt es so. → 6.6

Veröffentlichen und zurückkommen
GitHub Pages, ein Webspace über SFTP, rsync oder FTP, ein Ordner, ein Webhook, mit einer Vorschau
dessen, was übertragen wird. Und vor größeren Änderungen ein Snapshot, zu dem man zurückkehren
kann. → 6.7, 7.2
